                  [0-1136] StaticText: is the capital of the
                  [0-1137] link: Netherlands
                  [0-1139] StaticText: . It is known for the canals that cross the city, its impressive architecture, museums and art galleries, its notorious red light district, and more than 1,500 bridges.
                [0-1140] paragraph
                  [0-1141] StaticText: The city has earned the title of
                  [0-1142] StaticText: Venice of the North
                  [0-1143] StaticText: for a good reason: few other cities have intricate web of canals, exquisite architecture, and a staggering collection of over 1500 bridges weave an undeniable charm.                 [0-772] paragraph
                  [0-1144] StaticText: Although once an innocuous and humble fishing village during the late 12th century, Amsterdam catapulted into global prominence during the 17th century as a bustling trading hub. The 19th and 20th centuries ushered in expansion, punctuated by modernist districts.

                [0-1294] paragraph
                  [0-1295] StaticText: With a population surpassing 934,000 in 2025 – and soaring well past a million when you account for the immediate surroundings – Amsterdam unquestionably holds the crown as the Netherlands' largest city. Numbers aside, Amsterdam is the financial, cultural, and creative heart of the nation. English is widely spoken and understood by almost everyone, so language barriers are rarely an issue for travellers.
                [0-1296] region: Orientation
                  [0-6441] div
                    [0-1297] heading: Orientation
                    [0-1299] link: edit
                  [0-1301] figure

                      [0-1303] StaticText: Corner of Keizersgracht and Reguliersgracht
                  [0-1304] paragraph
                    [0-1305] StaticText: The "Amsterdam" that most visitors experience is the city centre, the semi-circle with Centraal Station at its apex. It corresponds to the city as it was around 1850. Five major concentric canals ring the Binnenstad: Singel, Herengracht, Keizersgracht, Prinsengracht and Singelgracht, together forming the Canal District. Other districts inside the city centre are the Jordaan, a former working class area now popular with yuppies, and Plantage, a leafy and spacious area with botanical gardens and the zoo. The Nassaukade, Stadhouderskade and Mauritskade surround the city centre and mark the location of the former city moat and fortifications. Almost everything outside this line was built after 1870.
                  [0-1306] paragraph
                    [0-1307] StaticText: The semi-circle is on the south side of the IJ, which is often called a river but more exactly is an estuary. Going east from Centraal Station, the railway passes the artificial islands of the redeveloped Eastern Docklands. North of the IJ is mainly housing, although a major dockland redevelopment has started there too.
                  [0-1308] paragraph
                    [0-1309] StaticText: The river Amstel flows into the city from the south. Originally, it flowed along the line Rokin-Damrak. The dam in the Amstel, which gives the city its name, was located under the present Bijenkorf department store near Dam Square. The original settlement was on the right bank of the Amstel, on the present Warmoesstraat: it is therefore the oldest street in the city. The city has expanded in all directions, except to the northeast of the A10 ring motorway. That area is a protected rural landscape of open fields and small villages considered a part of the Waterland region.
                  [0-1310] paragraph
                    [0-1311] StaticText: The radius of the semi-circle is about 2
                    [0-1312] StaticText: 
                    [0-1313] StaticText: km. All major tourist destinations, and most hotels, are located inside it or just outside it. As a result, a large swathe of Amsterdam is not visited by the average tourist: at least 90% of the population lives outside this area. Most economic activity in Amsterdam—the offices of the financial sector, the port—is near or outside the ring motorway, which is 4–5
                    [0-1314] StaticText: 
                    [0-1315] StaticText: km from the centre.
                  [0-1316] paragraph
                    [0-1317] StaticText: The expansion of Amsterdam outside the ring motorway and the expansion of activity outside the city centre is redefining what locals consider the 'central area' of Amsterdam. Zuid, especially with the construction of the Noord/Zuidlijn and the Zuidas, is becoming more and more important in the daily lives of the locals. Its significance for tourists has increased by the now completed reconstruction work on the Museumplein and the adjoining museums.

                    [0-1329] StaticText: ("dam on the Amstel") in 1204, and known as
                    [0-1330] StaticText: Aemsterdam
                    [0-1331] StaticText: by 1327. It was first part of Utrecht, and around 1300 Gwijde van Henegouwen, bishop of Utrecht, gave Amsterdam city rights. After his death, the city was inherited by Count William III and became a part of Holland. Two fires swept the city in 1421 and 1452, and few wooden buildings from this period remain. A notable exception is the
                    [0-1332] StaticText: Houten Huis
                    [0-1333] StaticText: (Wooden House) at the Begijnhof.
                  [0-1334] paragraph
                    [0-1335] StaticText: In 1558, the Dutch started to revolt against the Spanish as the local nobility demanded more political power and religious freedom. Amsterdam supported the Spanish, but as it became more and more isolated and trade suffered accordingly, it switched sides in 1578. A relative freedom of religion emerged in the newly established Dutch Republic, and many migrants sought refuge in Amsterdam, including Jews from the Iberian Peninsula, merchants from Antwerp and
                    [0-1336] StaticText: Huguenots
                    [0-1337] StaticText: (French Protestants). Catholicism could not be practiced openly.
                  [0-1338] paragraph
                    [0-1339] StaticText: Amsterdam prospered in the 17th century and became one of the world's great cities. A global trading network and overseas possessions made Amsterdam the centre of shipping in Europe and the world's leading financial centre. The arts flourished too, with great painters like Rembrandt producing works that are widely acclaimed as of this day. The city expanded outside of its original boundaries as the Canal Belt was constructed for wealthy merchants and the Jordaan for the working class. Immigrants formed the majority of the population and there was a strong immigration from Lutheran Protestant Germans.
                  [0-1340] paragraph
                    [0-1341] StaticText: The Dutch Republic was not a unitary state, but a confederation in which the independent provinces and the larger cities were politically autonomous. There was a strong animosity between the Orange faction with its power base in The Hague and the republican faction with Amsterdam as its most outspoken representative, up to the point that the city was beleaguered by the army. The Orange faction supported the idea of hereditary political leadership vested in the princes of Orange as Stadtholders, while the republican faction supported civic independence. This long-standing culture of republicanism and non-conformism against the political elites in The Hague exists to this day.
                  [0-1342] figure
                    [0-1343] link
                      [0-641] image
                    [0-6472] Figcaption
                      [0-1344] StaticText: Royal Palace
                  [0-1345] paragraph
                    [0-1346] StaticText: The 18th and 19th centuries were a turbulent period for Amsterdam. The economy suffered from decreased trade opportunities with the colonies and ongoing wars with the United Kingdom and France. Napoleon's brother Louis was crowned King of Holland in 1806 and took possession of the city hall on Dam Square, from then on referred to as the Royal Palace. The Netherlands was fully annexed by France in 1810, and Napoleon crowned Amsterdam "third city" of the French Empire. Prussian and Russian troops liberated the Netherlands, but it remained a unitary state and a monarchy, that now included Belgium.
                  [0-1347] paragraph
                    [0-1348] StaticText: While The Hague had functioned as
                    [0-1349] StaticText: de facto
                    [0-1350] StaticText: capital of the Republic, Amsterdam (together with Brussels) became the new capital of the Kingdom.                 [0-1134] paragraph
                  [0-1135] StaticText: Amsterdam
                  [0-1136] StaticText: is the capital of the
                  [0-1137] link: Netherlands
                  [0-1139] StaticText: . It is known for the canals that cross the city, its impressive architecture, museums and art galleries, its notorious red light district, and more than 1,500 bridges.
                [0-1140] paragraph
                  [0-1141] StaticText: The city has earned the title of
                  [0-1142] StaticText: Venice of the North
                  [0-1143] StaticText: for a good reason: few other cities have intricate web of canals, exquisite architecture, and a staggering collection of over 1500 bridges weave an undeniable charm. Whether you're here for the rich cultural heritage, the vibrant nightlife, or the serene alleyways, Amsterdam's magnetic pull is universal.
                [0-772] paragraph
                  [0-1144] StaticText: Although once an innocuous and humble fishing village during the late 12th century, Amsterdam catapulted into global prominence during the 17th century as a bustling trading hub. The city's evolution birthed iconic districts like Jordaan and the Canal Belt, the latter earning UNESCO World Heritage status in 2010. The 19th and 20th centuries ushered in expansion, punctuated by modernist districts.

                [0-1294] paragraph
                  [0-1295] StaticText: With a population surpassing 934,000 in 2025 – and soaring well past a million when you account for the immediate surroundings – Amsterdam unquestionably holds the crown as the Netherlands' largest city. Numbers aside, Amsterdam is the financial, cultural, and creative heart of the nation. English is widely spoken and understood by almost everyone, so language barriers are rarely an issue for travellers.
                [0-1296] region: Orientation
                  [0-6441] div
                    [0-1297] heading: Orientation
                    [0-1299] link: edit
                  [0-1301] figure
                    [0-1302] link
                      [0-639] image
                    [0-6451] Figcaption
                      [0-1303] StaticText: Corner of Keizersgracht and Reguliersgracht
                  [0-1304] paragraph
                    [0-1305] StaticText: The "Amsterdam" that most visitors experience is the city centre, the semi-circle with Centraal Station at its apex. It corresponds to the city as it was around 1850. Five major concentric canals ring the Binnenstad: Singel, Herengracht, Keizersgracht, Prinsengracht and Singelgracht, together forming the Canal District. Other districts inside the city centre are the Jordaan, a former working class area now popular with yuppies, and Plantage, a leafy and spacious area with botanical gardens and the zoo. The Nassaukade, Stadhouderskade and Mauritskade surround the city centre and mark the location of the former city moat and fortifications. Almost everything outside this line was built after 1870.
                  [0-1306] paragraph
                    [0-1307] StaticText: The semi-circle is on the south side of the IJ, which is often called a river but more exactly is an estuary. Going east from Centraal Station, the railway passes the artificial islands of the redeveloped Eastern Docklands. North of the IJ is mainly housing, although a major dockland redevelopment has started there too.
                  [0-1308] paragraph
                    [0-1309] StaticText: The river Amstel flows into the city from the south. Originally, it flowed along the line Rokin-Damrak. The dam in the Amstel, which gives the city its name, was located under the present Bijenkorf department store near Dam Square. The original settlement was on the right bank of the Amstel, on the present Warmoesstraat: it is therefore the oldest street in the city. The city has expanded in all directions, except to the northeast of the A10 ring motorway. That area is a protected rural landscape of open fields and small villages considered a part of the Waterland region.
                  [0-1310] paragraph
                    [0-1311] StaticText: The radius of the semi-circle is about 2
                    [0-1312] StaticText: 
                    [0-1313] StaticText: km. All major tourist destinations, and most hotels, are located inside it or just outside it. As a result, a large swathe of Amsterdam is not visited by the average tourist: at least 90% of the population lives outside this area. Most economic activity in Amsterdam—the offices of the financial sector, the port—is near or outside the ring motorway, which is 4–5
                    [0-1314] StaticText: 
                    [0-1315] StaticText: km from the centre.
                  [0-1316] paragraph
                    [0-1317] StaticText: The expansion of Amsterdam outside the ring motorway and the expansion of activity outside the city centre is redefining what locals consider the 'central area' of Amsterdam. Zuid, especially with the construction of the Noord/Zuidlijn and the Zuidas, is becoming more and more important in the daily lives of the locals. Its significance for tourists has increased by the now completed reconstruction work on the Museumplein and the adjoining museums.
                [0-1318] region: History
                  [0-6455] div
                    [0-1319] heading: History
                    [0-1321] link: edit
                  [0-1323] figure
                    [0-1324] link
                      [0-642] image
                    [0-6465] Figcaption
                      [0-1325] StaticText: Begijnhof
                  [0-1326] paragraph
                    [0-1327] StaticText: Amsterdam was first referred to as
                    [0-1328] StaticText: Aemstelledamme
                    [0-1329] StaticText: ("dam on the Amstel") in 1204, and known as
                    [0-1330] StaticText: Aemsterdam
                    [0-1331] StaticText: by 1327. It was first part of Utrecht, and around 1300 Gwijde van Henegouwen, bishop of Utrecht, gave Amsterdam city rights. After his death, the city was inherited by Count William III and became a part of Holland. Two fires swept the city in 1421 and 1452, and few wooden buildings from this period remain. A notable exception is the
                    [0-1332] StaticText: Houten Huis
                    [0-1333] StaticText: (Wooden House) at the Begijnhof.
                  [0-1334] paragraph
                    [0-1335] StaticText: In 1558, the Dutch started to revolt against the Spanish as the local nobility demanded more political power and religious freedom. Amsterdam supported the Spanish, but as it became more and more isolated and trade suffered accordingly, it switched sides in 1578. A relative freedom of religion emerged in the newly established Dutch Republic, and many migrants sought refuge in Amsterdam, including Jews from the Iberian Peninsula, merchants from Antwerp and
                    [0-1336] StaticText: Huguenots
                    [0-1337] StaticText: (French Protestants). Catholicism could not be practiced openly.
                  [0-1338] paragraph
                    [0-1339] StaticText: Amsterdam prospered in the 17th century and became one of the world's great cities. A global trading network and overseas possessions made Amsterdam the centre of shipping in Europe and the world's leading financial centre. The arts flourished too, with great painters like Rembrandt producing works that are widely acclaimed as of this day. The city expanded outside of its original boundaries as the Canal Belt was constructed for wealthy merchants and the Jordaan for the working class. Immigrants formed the majority of the population and there was a strong immigration from Lutheran Protestant Germans.
                  [0-1340] paragraph
                    [0-1341] StaticText: The Dutch Republic was not a unitary state, but a confederation in which the independent provinces and the larger cities were politically autonomous. There was a strong animosity between the Orange faction with its power base in The Hague and the republican faction with Amsterdam as its most outspoken representative, up to the point that the city was beleaguered by the army. The Orange faction supported the idea of hereditary political leadership vested in the princes of Orange as Stadtholders, while the republican faction supported civic independence. This long-standing culture of republicanism and non-conformism against the political elites in The Hague exists to this day.
                  [0-1342] figure
                    [0-1343] link
                      [0-641] image
                    [0-6472] Figcaption
                      [0-1344] StaticText: Royal Palace
                  [0-1345] paragraph
                    [0-1346] StaticText: The 18th and 19th centuries were a turbulent period for Amsterdam. The economy suffered from decreased trade opportunities with the colonies and ongoing wars with the United Kingdom and France. Napoleon's brother Louis was crowned King of Holland in 1806 and took possession of the city hall on Dam Square, from then on referred to as the Royal Palace. The Netherlands was fully annexed by France in 1810, and Napoleon crowned Amsterdam "third city" of the French Empire. Prussian and Russian troops liberated the Netherlands, but it remained a unitary state and a monarchy, that now included Belgium.
                  [0-1347] paragraph
                    [0-1348] StaticText: While The Hague had functioned as
                    [0-1349] StaticText: de facto
                    [0-1350] StaticText: capital of the Republic, Amsterdam (together with Brussels) became the new capital of the Kingdom. The appointment of Amsterdam as the new capital was a conciliatory gesture of the Orange faction towards the city and a recognition of the strong civic and republican basis of the new Kingdom. The Hague remained the seat of government and the political centre of the country. When Belgium seceded in 1830, Amsterdam became the sole capital and got the rights to trade with the country's overseas possessions.
                  [0-1351] paragraph
                    [0-1352] StaticText: The North Sea Canal and Noordhollandsch Kanaal connected Amsterdam's harbour directly with the Rhine and the North Sea. The Industrial Revolution arrived around 1860, which led to strong economic growth, but also to overpopulation as the city could not cope with the sudden demographic surge. The Jordaan was a notorious working class slum in this period, and neighbourhoods like De Pijp were built to provide housing as cheaply and quickly as possible for the lower middle class. Social issues that arose in this period made Amsterdam the centre of social democracy in the country.
                  [0-1353] paragraph
                    [0-1354] StaticText: In World War II, German troops occupied the city and more than 100,000 Jews were deported to death camps, most famously Anne Frank. The diamond trade, before the war one of Amsterdam's top industries, almost completely disappeared as these businesses were mostly in the hands of Jews. The cultural revolution of the 1960s and 1970s changed Amsterdam radically. Soft drugs were tolerated, squatting became commonplace and riots with the police occurred on a daily basis. The coronation of Queen Beatrix in 1980 turned violent as protesters demanded a stop to the housing demolition that took place for the construction of Amsterdam's first metro line.
                  [0-1355] paragraph
                    [0-1356] StaticText: In subsequent decades, Amsterdam has lost some of its revolutionary appeal, becoming a centre for wealthy yuppies. Once poor districts like the Jordaan became upper class districts, and poorer inhabitants moved out of the centre to the outer boroughs and other cities. The city's once progressive ideals have faded as squatting is cracked down on, coffeeshops are increasingly closed and prostitution is outlawed outside of the Red Light District. However, it is still a progressive and tolerant city by international standards. Its culture of republicanism and non-conformism are going through tough times as well, but the ubiquitous "Republic of Amsterdam" street signs show that it remains a defining characteristic of the city.

                  [0-1748] paragraph
                    [0-1749] StaticText: Amsterdam is a large city and a major tourist destination, so you can visit it all year round. However, in winter the days are short (8
                    [0-1750] StaticText: 
                    [0-1751] StaticText: hours of daylight around Christmas between 08:45 and 16:30), and the weather may be too cold to walk around the city comfortably, let alone cycle. January and February are the coldest months, with lows around
                    [0-1752] StaticText: 0
                    [0-1753] StaticText: 
                    [0-1754] StaticText: °C (32
                    [0-1755] StaticText: 
                    [0-1756] StaticText: °F)
                    [0-1757] StaticText: and highs around
                    [0-1758] StaticText: 5
                    [0-1759] StaticText: 
                    [0-1760] StaticText: °C (41
                    [0-1761] StaticText: 
                    [0-1762] StaticText: °F)
                    [0-1763] StaticText: . Snow does occur a few times each winter, but it's often light and rarely stays on the ground more than a couple of days.
                  [0-1764] paragraph
                    [0-1765] StaticText: In summer, heat waves (3 days above
                    [0-1766] StaticText: 30
                    [0-1767] StaticText: 
                    [0-1768] StaticText: °C (86
                    [0-1769] StaticText: 
                    [0-1770] StaticText: °F)
                    [0-1771] StaticText: ) are common, as is a temperature of
                    [0-1772] StaticText: 18
                    [0-1773] StaticText: 
                    [0-1774] StaticText: °C (64
                    [0-1775] StaticText: 
                    [0-1776] StaticText: °F)
                    [0-1777] StaticText: with rainfall. July and August are the warmest months, with an average temperature of
                    [0-1778] StaticText: 22
                    [0-1779] StaticText: 
                    [0-1780] StaticText: °C (72
                    [0-1781] StaticText: 
                    [0-1782] StaticText: °F)
                    [0-1783] StaticText: at daytime and
                    [0-1784] StaticText: 14
                    [0-1785] StaticText: 
                    [0-1786] StaticText: °C (57
                    [0-1787] StaticText: 
                    [0-1788] StaticText: °F)
                    [0-1789] StaticText: at night. Days with very high temperatures above
                    [0-1790] StaticText: 27
                    [0-1791] StaticText: 
                    [0-1792] StaticText: °C (81
                    [0-1793] StaticText: 
                    [0-1794] StaticText: °F)
                    [0-1795] StaticText: are often followed with nights around or above
                    [0-1796] StaticText: 17
                    [0-1797] StaticText: 
                    [0-1798] StaticText: °C (63
                    [0-1799] StaticText: 
                    [0-1800] StaticText: °F)
                    [0-1801] StaticText: . Sunsets are as late as 22:00 and sunrise is around 05:30 during the summer.
                  [0-1802] paragraph
                    [0-1803] StaticText: Neither summer nor winter constantly have the mentioned values. Always be prepared for rain. On average, it's raining one in every two days, but it might well be raining the full week of your trip if you visit during winter. Gray clouds cover Amsterdam most of the time, but in spring and summer the sun shines six to eight hours a day on average.
                  [0-1804] paragraph
                    [0-1805] StaticText: King's Day (
                    [0-1806] StaticText: Koningsdag
                    [0-1807] StaticText: ) is always celebrated on 27 April, unless this date occurs on a Sunday (then it's celebrated the Saturday before). The weather on King's Day is usually quite good, with temperatures hovering around
                    [0-1808] StaticText: 17
                    [0-1809] StaticText: 
                    [0-1810] StaticText: °C (63
                    [0-1811] StaticText: 
                    [0-1812] StaticText: °F)
                    [0-1813] StaticText: . If it's raining, there will be considerably fewer people on the streets.

                  [0-2324] paragraph
                    [0-2325] StaticText: There are only a few long-distance national bus services in the Netherlands, and apparently none to Amsterdam Centraal. Bus 300 connects
                    [0-2326] link: Haarlem
                    [0-2328] StaticText: train station with Hoofddorp, Schiphol Airport, Amstelveen and Amsterdam Bijlmer ArenA.
                [0-2329] region: By car
                  [0-7313] div
                    [0-2330] heading: By car
                    [0-2332] link: edit
                  [0-2334] paragraph
                    [0-2335] StaticText: The western part of the Netherlands has a dense (and congested) road network. Coming from the east (Germany), motorway
                    [0-2336] link
                      [0-2337] image
                    [0-2338] StaticText: directly leads to Amsterdam. If you're taking motorway A12 from Arnhem, change in Utrecht onto the A2 in the northern direction. From the south (Belgium), follow motorways A16, A27 and A2, in that order in northern direction. From The Hague, the A4 leads to Amsterdam. All motorways to Amsterdam connect to the Ring motorway, the A10. From this motorway, main roads lead radially into Amsterdam (the roads S101 through S118).
                  [0-2339] paragraph
                    [0-2340] StaticText: In most cases, you'll want to avoid getting into the area enclosed by the ring road. Traffic is dense and parking spaces are expensive and difficult to find. Instead, when on the A10, follow the signs to one of the
                    [0-2341] link: P+R-spots
                    [0-2344] StaticText: (P+R Zeeburg to the east, P+R Johan Cruijff ArenA to the southeast, P+R Olympisch Stadion to the south, P+R Noord to the north, and P+R Sloterdijk to the west). Here you can park your car and take public transport to the city centre. There is a rate of
                    [0-7324] Abbr: €8-13 ≈ US$9.2–14.9, UK£6.9–11.3, CA$13–21.1, AU$13–21.3, NZ$16–26
                      [0-2345] StaticText: €8-13
                    [0-2346] StaticText: a day. To benefit from the discounted rate, you need to use a OV-chipkaart or disposable GVB OV-chipkaart: OVpay or QR-tickets are not accepted. Please note: the last check-in or transfer must be within the city centre zone. You can park for free at a few places that have metro or tram stops nearby (e.g. IKEA near metro station Bullewijk).
                  [0-2347] paragraph
                    [0-2348] StaticText: The speed limit on Dutch motorways is 100
                    [0-2349] StaticText: 
                    [0-2350] StaticText: km/h during the day and 130
                    [0-2351] StaticText: 
                    [0-2352] StaticText: km/h during the night, except where indicated. On the A10 ring motorway around Amsterdam, the maximum speed is 100
                    [0-2353] StaticText: 
                    [0-2354] StaticText: km/h, and 80
                    [0-2355] StaticText: 
                    [0-2356] StaticText: km/h on the Western section. These limits are strictly enforced and there are many speed cameras.
                [0-2357] region: By boat
                  [0-7329] div
                    [0-2358] heading: By boat
                    [0-2360] link: edit
                  [0-2362] paragraph
                    [0-2363] StaticText: The
                    [0-7339] span
                      [0-2364] link: 6
                      [0-2366] StaticText: Passenger Terminal Amsterdam
                    [0-2367] StaticText: is close to the city centre but is only used for cruise ships. The nearest ferry port is
                    [0-2368] link: IJmuiden
                    [0-2370] StaticText: , where ferries from Newcastle upon Tyne dock.
                    [0-2371] link: DFDS Seaways
                    [0-2373] StaticText: offers daily overnight ferry services from Newcastle upon Tyne (more specifically, North Shields) in the United Kingdom.
                  [0-2374] paragraph
                    [0-2375] StaticText: Other ferry services dock at Rotterdam Europoort (ferry from Hull) and Hook of Holland (ferry from Harwich). These are about 70
                    [0-2376] StaticText: 
                    [0-2377] StaticText: km away from Amsterdam. Intercity and Intercity Direct trains run direct from Amsterdam Centraal to Rotterdam Centraal every 10 to 15
                    [0-2378] StaticText: 
                    [0-2379] StaticText: minutes taking approximately 1
                    [0-2380] StaticText: 
                    [0-2381] StaticText: hr 15
                    [0-2382] StaticText: 
                    [0-2383] StaticText: min. See the National train operator NS website for booking and information.
                  [0-2384] paragraph
                    [0-2385] StaticText: For the Stena Line ferry to Harwich: from Rotterdam Centraal, change for Rotterdam Metro Line B direct to Hoek Van Holland Station where you will be able to walk onto the Ferry. See Rotterdam RET website for tickets and information. For P&O to Hull: there is no public transport however Taxis are readily available at Rotterdam Centraal. P&O offer some coach options via their website.
              [0-2386] region: Get around
                [0-7353] div
                  [0-2387] heading: Get around
                  [0-2389] link: edit
                [0-2391] paragraph
                  [0-2392] StaticText: Amsterdam's city centre is quite compact, and pretty flat, so you can easily get to most tourist destinations
                  [0-2393] StaticText: on foot
                  [0-2394] StaticText: . From Amsterdam Centraal, most areas in the city centre can be reached within half an hour.
                [0-2395] paragraph
                  [0-2396] StaticText: Public transport within the city is operated by the
                  [0-2397] link: GVB
                  [0-2399] StaticText: . The tram is the main form of public transport and there is a metro and dozens of bus routes. Most routes operate from 06:00 (06:30 Saturdays and 07:45 Sundays) until around midnight. There are a few overnight bus routes as well. Regional buses, and some suburban buses, are operated by
                  [0-2400] link: Connexxion
                  [0-2402] StaticText: and
                  [0-2403] link: EBS
                  [0-2405] StaticText: .
                [0-2406] region: Tickets
                  [0-7364] div
                    [0-2407] heading: Tickets
                    [0-2409] link: edit
                  [0-2411] paragraph
                    [0-2412] StaticText: For many years, an
                    [0-2413] link: OV-chipkaart
                    [0-2415] StaticText: provided the only way to pay transportation fees in the city. However, as of 2023, fees may be paid at the station or on the tram, bus, or NS train by using a contactless
                    [0-2416] link: credit or debit card
                    [0-9470] StaticText: 
                    [0-2418] StaticText: (OVpay)
                    [0-2419] StaticText: either on a card or on a mobile device. Many travellers find their bank card easier than buying and keeping track of an
                    [0-2420] StaticText: OV-chipkaart
                    [0-2421] StaticText: , as they do not have to obtain, maintain, and monitor the balance on the contactless card. User procedures (tapping in and out) on both kinds of cards are the same. To travel with a contactless card or an
                    [0-2422] StaticText: OV-chipkaart
                    [0-2423] StaticText: , you have to check in at the start of your journey and check out at the end by holding the card in front of the card reader.
                  [0-2424] region: Alternative payment options
                    [0-7378] div
                      [0-2425] heading: Alternative payment options
                      [0-2427] link: edit
                    [0-2429] paragraph
                      [0-2430] StaticText: Besides using a debit or credit card, you have other options: an OV-chipkaart, an OV-pas or the GVB app.
                    [0-2431] paragraph
                      [0-2432] StaticText: Three types of
                      [0-2433] StaticText: OV-chipkaart
                      [0-2434] StaticText: are available:
                    [0-2435] list
                      [0-2436] listitem
                        [0-7388] ListMarker: •
                        [0-2437] StaticText: Personal card
                        [0-2438] StaticText: on which you can load money and weekly, monthly, or yearly subscriptions. You can also load GVB hours, day and multi-day tickets on the card.
                      [0-2439] listitem
                        [0-7390] ListMarker: •
                        [0-2440] StaticText: Anonymous card
                        [0-2441] StaticText: on which you can load money that can be spent on public transport
                      [0-2442] listitem
                        [0-7392] ListMarker: •
                        [0-2443] StaticText: Disposable card
                        [0-2444] StaticText: that can be used for a limited period of time (an hour or a few days)
                    [0-2445] paragraph
                      [0-2446] StaticText: The first two types of cards come with no credit included and cost
                      [0-7394] Abbr: €7.50 ≈ US$8.6, UK£6.5, CA$12.2, AU$12.3, NZ$15
                        [0-2447] StaticText: €7.50
                      [0-2448] StaticText: and expires after 5 years. To travel in the city you have to top up such a card for at least
                      [0-7395] Abbr: €4 ≈ US$4.6, UK£3.5, CA$6.5, AU$6.5, NZ$8
                        [0-2449] StaticText: €4
                      [0-2450] StaticText: before a journey begins. A
                      [0-2451] StaticText: disposable
                      [0-2452] StaticText: card, on the other hand, already has a
                      [0-2453] StaticText: product
                      [0-2454] StaticText: bundled with it, but it can not be re-used after this product expires.
                    [0-2455] paragraph
                      [0-2456] StaticText: Anonymous and disposable
                      [0-2457] StaticText: OV-chipkaarts
                      [0-2458] StaticText: can be obtained from GVB vending machines in most metro stations (cash only, except on line 52), from the desks at some larger stations (including Amsterdam Centraal) and some shops. Additionally 1-hour disposable cards can be bought on a tram at the tram conductor but only PIN (debit and credit) cards are accepted to purchase them on board. After purchasing disposable cards from the tram conductor, you must check in and check out with that card.
                    [0-2459] paragraph
                      [0-2460] StaticText: The OV-pas is being phased in since 2025 as a replacement for the OV-Chipkaart and is only available as a personal card. The OV-pas is slightly cheaper than the OV-Chipkaart
                      [0-7399] Abbr: €6.00 ≈ US$6.9, UK£5.2, CA$9.7, AU$9.8, NZ$12
                        [0-2461] StaticText: €6.00
                      [0-2462] StaticText: and also expires after 5 years.
                    [0-2463] paragraph
                      [0-2464] StaticText: Tickets can also be purchased through the GVB mobile app - just scan the QR code on your mobile at the card reader.
                  [0-2465] region: Season tickets

                      [0-2466] heading: Season tickets
                      [0-2468] link: edit
                    [0-2470] paragraph
                      [0-2471] StaticText: For those who stay in Amsterdam longer, one of the
                      [0-2472] link: day or multi-day passes
                      [0-2474] StaticText: could be a useful option. You can get them for 24
                      [0-2475] StaticText: 
                      [0-2476] StaticText: hours up to 168
                      [0-2477] StaticText: 
                      [0-2478] StaticText: hours. This allows the holder to travel on an unlimited number of journeys on the tram, metro and bus throughout the validity period of the pass. Travel passes can be loaded on the anonymous cards but existing credit on such cards cannot be applied towards the purchase of a pass. These passes are not valid on buses operated by Connexxion, EBS and Keolis. These passes can be purchased at tourist offices (at Schiphol Airport and just outside Amsterdam Centraal), many hotels and GVB ticket offices. Additionally, a one-day pass can be purchased from the conductor on a tram (but not on a bus).

                [0-2590] region: By metro
                  [0-7484] div
                    [0-2591] heading: By metro
                    [0-2593] link: edit
                  [0-2595] figure
                    [0-2596] link
                      [0-635] image
                    [0-7494] Figcaption
                      [0-2597] StaticText: Amsterdam Metro Map
                  [0-2598] paragraph
                    [0-2599] StaticText: There are five
                    [0-2600] StaticText: metro
                    [0-2601] StaticText: lines in Amsterdam, including a short underground section in the city centre, that serves the suburbs. It takes 15–20
                    [0-2602] StaticText: 
                    [0-2603] StaticText: minutes from Centraal Station to Zuid or Bijlmer ArenA in Zuidoost. However, in practice, M50, M51 and M53 all act as branch lines of M54 (including sharing the same tracks). The 5th metro line, the Noord/Zuidlijn (M52 North–South Line), finally opened in 2018, and the only line to functionally act as a separate line. It's an underground metro line that connects the north of Amsterdam directly with the south of the city through the city centre, hence the name.
                [0-2604] region: By tram
                  [0-7498] div
                    [0-2605] heading: By tram
                    [0-2607] link: edit
                  [0-2609] figure
                    [0-2610] link
                      [0-640] image
                    [0-7508] Figcaption
                      [0-2611] StaticText: Amsterdam tram & metro system
                  [0-2612] paragraph
                    [0-2613] StaticText: The tram network has 15 lines and it is considered the major carrier in the central area of the city. Amsterdam Centraal is the largest hub of the tram system with 8 tram lines terminating there.
                    [0-7511] span
                      [0-2614] link: 7
                      [0-2616] StaticText: Leidseplein
                    [0-2617] StaticText: is the next largest hub with 7 tram lines passing through. Tram lines 5 and 25 serve the neighbouring municipality of
                    [0-2618] link: Amstelveen
                    [0-2620] StaticText: , and tram line 19 serves the neighbouring municipality of
                    [0-2621] link: Diemen
                    [0-2623] StaticText: . Many metro stations provide connections with nearby tram lines.
                  [0-2624] paragraph
                    [0-2625] StaticText: All tram stops have a detailed map of the system and the surrounding area. You can also get a free public transport map at the GVB ticket office (just outside Amsterdam Centraal).
                  [0-2626] paragraph
                    [0-2627] StaticText: Most trams these days have conductors, near the rear of the tram. Board by the driver or the conductor. If you have questions, the conductor will be sure to respond to your query. You can buy 1-hour, 24-hour, and 48-hour tickets from the conductors.
                [0-2628] region: By bus
                  [0-7521] div
                    [0-2629] heading: By bus
                    [0-2631] link: edit
                  [0-2633] paragraph
                    [0-2634] StaticText: Just like the tram and metro, local buses are operated by the GVB. There are also suburban buses to nearby towns such as Haarlem and Uithoorn; these are operated by Connexxion or EBS (the company name and house style is prominent on the bus side) and can be used within Amsterdam if you travel with an
                    [0-2635] StaticText: OV-chipkaart
                    [0-2636] StaticText: or
                    [0-2637] StaticText: OVpay
                    [0-2638] StaticText: . Enter buses only via the front door. Generally, almost all bus routes operate very frequently throughout the week.
                [0-2639] region: By boat
                  [0-7532] div
                    [0-2640] heading: By boat
                    [0-2642] link: edit
                  [0-2644] paragraph
                    [0-2645] StaticText: There are several
                    [0-2646] StaticText: ferry
                    [0-2647] StaticText: services across the IJ river, between the city centre and Noord, the most frequent runs every 7
                    [0-2648] StaticText: 
                    [0-2649] StaticText: minutes. They all leave from a new jetty on the northern (rear) side of Amsterdam Centraal. All ferries are free of charge and provide nice views of the harbour and skyline.
                  [0-2650] paragraph
                    [0-2651] StaticText: The nicest one is the 15-min service to the NDSM-werf, a funky, up and coming, industrial neighbourhood with a nice cafe-bar (IJkantine), restaurant (Noorderlicht), indoor skateboard park, and the Pancake Boat (
                    [0-2652] StaticText: Pannenkoekenboot
                    [0-2653] StaticText: ) which sails many times each week. Ferries leave every 30
                    [0-2654] StaticText: 
                    [0-2655] StaticText: minutes from Amsterdam Centraal and from the NDSM-werf. Double frequencies during rush hours.
                  [0-2656] paragraph
                    [0-2657] StaticText: You can also hop on the ferry to Buiksloterweg, and then make a short walk to the EYE Film Institute for its architecture and free exhibition in the basement.
                [0-2658] region: By bicycle
                  [0-7545] div
                    [0-2659] heading: By bicycle
                    [0-2661] link: edit
                  [0-2663] paragraph
                    [0-2664] StaticText: A pleasant way to cover a lot of ground is to rent a
                    [0-2665] StaticText: bicycle
                    [0-2666] StaticText: . There are approximately 750,000 people living in Amsterdam and they own about 800,000 bicycles. The city is very, very bike-friendly, and there are separate bike lanes on most major streets. In the city centre, however, there is often not enough space for a bike lane, so cars and cyclists share narrow streets.
                  [0-2667] paragraph
                    [0-2668] StaticText: Cycling is the main mode of transport for most locals in the city and traffic is high paced. Be mindful of your surroundings and consider that if you don't have much experience cycling, you might be more comfortable using public transport or walking.
                  [0-2669] paragraph
                    [0-2670] StaticText: Cyclists do not have the right of way even though it might appear like that when observing the typical Amsterdammer's cycling behaviour. Be very careful and watch out for other cyclists. Always show other traffic where you're going (e.g. by holding out your hand) in order to avoid accidents and smoothen the traffic flow. If not indicated otherwise by signs, the right-before-left rule applies.
                  [0-2671] paragraph
                    [0-2672] StaticText: Avoid getting your tyre in the tram rails; it's a nasty fall. Always cross tram rails at an angle. When crossing tram lines, watch out for fast-approaching taxis, which have a rather ruthless driving style. Let none of the above deter you from doing it the Amsterdam way. Rent a bike! There are bike rental shops at railway stations and several others in and around the city centre. Bikes cost about
                    [0-7555] Abbr: €9 ≈ US$10, UK£7.8, CA$15, AU$15, NZ$18
                      [0-2673] StaticText: €9
                    [0-2674] StaticText: to
                    [0-7556] Abbr: €20 ≈ US$23, UK£17, CA$32, AU$33, NZ$40
                      [0-2675] StaticText: €20
                    [0-2676] StaticText: per day. Bring wet gear.
                  [0-2677] paragraph
                    [0-2678] StaticText: A good map for cycling routes, repairs, rentals and also public transport is
                    [0-2679] StaticText: Amsterdam op de fiets
                    [0-2680] StaticText: (a Cito-plan). Bicycles can be taken for free on all ferries across the IJ, on all metros, and on some carriages of tram 26 with a bike supplement fee on the
                    [0-2681] StaticText: OV-chipkaart
                    [0-2682] StaticText: (
                    [0-7559] Abbr: €2.20 ≈ US$2.52, UK£1.91, CA$3.57, AU$3.6, NZ$4.39
                      [0-2683] StaticText: €2.20
                    [0-2684] StaticText: in 2025, not allowed in rush hours). Use the special bike racks, locations indicated by a bicycle sign on the outside of the carriage.
                  [0-2685] paragraph
                    [0-2686] StaticText: Make sure to get a good lock (or two), and to use it. Amsterdam has one of the highest bicycle theft rates in the world. If you are buying a bike, prices that seem too good to be true are stolen bikes. Any bike offered for sale to passers-by, on the street, is certainly stolen. There's an old Amsterdam joke: when calling out to a large group of cyclists passing by "Hey, that's my bike!" about five people will jump off "their" bikes and start running.

                  [0-2809] paragraph
                    [0-2810] StaticText: The bicycle is a good way to explore the surrounding countryside. Within half an hour you're out of town. Go north, take the ferry across the IJ and cycle to
                    [0-2811] link: Waterland
                    [0-2813] StaticText: . Or go south, into the
                    [0-2814] link: Amsterdamse Bos
                    [0-2816] StaticText: , a giant park, or follow the river
                    [0-2817] StaticText: Amstel
                    [0-2818] StaticText: where Rembrandt worked. You can also take your bike onto the metro to the end of line station
                    [0-2819] StaticText: Gaasperplas
                    [0-2820] StaticText: , and cycle along rivers and windmills to old fortified towns like
                    [0-2821] link: Weesp
                    [0-2823] StaticText: ,
                    [0-2824] link: Muiden
                    [0-2826] StaticText: and
                    [0-2827] link: Naarden
                    [0-2829] StaticText: .
                [0-2830] region: By e-hailing
                  [0-7689] div
                    [0-2831] heading: By e-hailing
                    [0-2833] link: edit
                  [0-2835] paragraph
                    [0-2836] StaticText: The ride-hailing services of Uber and Bolt are available in Amsterdam. With them you can avoid a lot of the problems associated with taking an Amsterdam taxi from busy areas (Centraal Station/Leidseplein) and at peak evening hours.
                [0-2837] region: By taxi
                  [0-7698] div
                    [0-2838] heading: By taxi
                    [0-2840] link: edit
                  [0-2842] paragraph
                    [0-2843] StaticText: Taxis in Amsterdam are plentiful but expensive. Hailing taxis on the street is generally not to be recommended unless you are going to a well-known destination (e.g. Centraal Station or Schiphol). The liberalization of the taxi market in Amsterdam led to an influx of taxi drivers who have little or no clue of where they are going and who drive erratically and dangerously (e.g., driving on bicycle lanes instead of the main road or ignoring red lights). Tourists are advised to stick to public transport if at all possible. Get into a taxi only if you know the route yourself and are able to give directions to the taxi driver and if you know roughly how much the journey ought to cost so you don't get cheated.
                  [0-2844] paragraph
                    [0-2845] StaticText: Some drivers, traditionally at Centraal Station or Leidseplein, will refuse short trips or will quote outrageously high fares, even though all taxis are metered. Even if you convince the driver to use the meter, he will often take a circuitous route that racks up
                    [0-7707] Abbr: €15 ≈ US$17.2, UK£13, CA$24.3, AU$24.5, NZ$30
                      [0-2846] StaticText: €15
                    [0-2847] StaticText: or more on the meter. For reference, no trip within the historic centre should cost more than
                    [0-7708] Abbr: €10 ≈ US$11, UK£8.7, CA$16, AU$16, NZ$20
                      [0-2848] StaticText: €10
                    [0-2849] StaticText: or so.
                  [0-2850] paragraph
                    [0-2851] StaticText: The Netherlands (and Amsterdam) is in the middle of a huge taxi liberalization scheme which has been jarring to all involved. After many missteps, the government has introduced an unusual pricing scheme. First you feel sticker shock as the initial fare is now
                    [0-7709] Abbr: €7.50 ≈ US$8.6, UK£6.5, CA$12.2, AU$12.3, NZ$15
                      [0-2852] StaticText: €7.50
                    [0-2853] StaticText: . Luckily, that includes the first 2 km of travel and there is no charge for waiting in traffic. If you need to run in somewhere, you need to negotiate a waiting fee with the driver. 50 cents per minute is customary.
                  [0-2854] paragraph
                    [0-2855] StaticText: Unlicensed, illegal cabbies operate mainly in Zuidoost. These aren't easily recognized as such, and most certainly don't drive Mercedes cars. They are known as
                    [0-2856] StaticText: snorders
                    [0-2857] StaticText: and most easily reached by mobile phone. Rides within Zuidoost (the Bijlmer) range from
                    [0-7711] Abbr: €2.50 ≈ US$2.87, UK£2.17, CA$4.06, AU$4.09, NZ$4.99
                      [0-2858] StaticText: €2.50
                    [0-2859] StaticText: to
                    [0-7712] Abbr: €5 ≈ US$5.7, UK£4.3, CA$8.1, AU$8.2, NZ$10
                      [0-2860] StaticText: €5
                    [0-2861] StaticText: , whereas Zuidoost-Centre can run up to
                    [0-7713] Abbr: €12.50 ≈ US$14.33, UK£10.83, CA$20.29, AU$20.43, NZ$24.96
                      [0-2862] StaticText: €12.50
                    [0-2863] StaticText: .
                    [0-2864] StaticText: Snorders
                    [0-2865] StaticText: have a shady reputation, so consider their services only if you are adventurous.
                  [0-2866] paragraph
                    [0-2867] link: Staxi
                    [0-2869] StaticText: offers fixed fares for every pre-booked taxi ride.
                [0-2870] region: By car
                  [0-7715] div
                    [0-2871] heading: By car
                    [0-2873] link: edit
                  [0-2875] paragraph
                    [0-2876] StaticText: Cars
                    [0-2877] StaticText: are anything but miserable torture only outside the historic centre; within the historic centre, public transport is by far your best bet. In Amsterdam, a car is generally a liability and not an asset, as traffic is dense and parking spaces are quite expensive and very hard to find. Use a car only if you are going to an obscure location many kilometers out that is not served by public transport, or during the less busy times of the day or week, you may want to park near the Centraal Station and take the tram or walk. Driving here is a pain: many of the streets are narrow, the traffic (and parking) signs are baroque and obscure, and cyclists and pedestrians may get in your way. Plus, petrol is about
                    [0-7725] Abbr: €1.54 ≈ US$1.766, UK£1.334, CA$2.499, AU$2.518, NZ$3.075
                      [0-2878] StaticText: €1.54
                    [0-2879] StaticText: to
                    [0-7726] Abbr: €1.7 ≈ US$1.95, UK£1.47, CA$2.76, AU$2.78, NZ$3.39
                      [0-2880] StaticText: €1.7
                    [0-2881] StaticText: per liter.
                  [0-2882] paragraph
                    [0-2883] StaticText: Parking on the street at the city centre can reach as much as
                    [0-7727] Abbr: €7.76 ≈ US$8.898, UK£6.724, CA$12.59, AU$12.69, NZ$15.49
                      [0-2884] StaticText: €7.76
                    [0-2885] StaticText: an hour (2025)! Luckily there is a cheaper way, specially if you are going to park for more than a couple of hours. Mobypark is a shared parking platform where you can find and book
                    [0-2886] link: parking in the centre of Amsterdam
                    [0-2888] StaticText: as well as some great P+R location like
                    [0-2889] link: RAI Amsterdam
                  [0-2891] paragraph
                    [0-2892] StaticText: You can also try parking at one of the secured parking garages, for example under Museumplein, or near Centraal Station, and then walk around the city centre, or get on a tram. Car parking is very expensive in Amsterdam and it's often hard to find a place to park. You can choose to pay by the hour or for the whole day. Parking is free outside the centre on Sunday—there is always a spot available on the Albert Cuypstraat (which is a market during the rest of the week). From there, it is a 5-minute tram ride or 15
                    [0-2893] StaticText: 
                    [0-2894] StaticText: minutes walk to the city centre.
                  [0-2895] paragraph
                    [0-2896] StaticText: You can park for free in some parts of Amsterdam outside the city centre though this is slowly changing. Parking is still free in some areas in Noord, and you can take metro 52 from Noord or Noorderpark to the city centre. Another option is to park your car outside the city centre at a Park and Ride facility, as described in the
                    [0-2897] link: Get in
                    [0-2899] StaticText: section.
                  [0-2900] paragraph
                    [0-2901] StaticText: Popular car rental chains operate in a smaller capacity in Amsterdam, including Avis and Budget.
                    [0-2902] link: Free2move
                    [0-2904] StaticText: has 400 all-electric cars available within and around the city.
                [0-2905] region: By ice skates
                  [0-7729] div
                    [0-2906] heading: By ice skates
                    [0-2908] link: edit
                  [0-2910] paragraph
                    [0-2911] StaticText: Ice skating is a longstanding tradition in the Netherlands, and you will sometimes see locals skating down the canals when they freeze over in the winter. However, the ice has to be thick enough for you to be able to do this safely, and this requires temperatures to stay below
                    [0-2912] StaticText: −5
                    [0-2913] StaticText: 
                    [0-2914] StaticText: °C (23
                    [0-2915] StaticText: 
                    [0-2916] StaticText: °F)
                    [0-2917] StaticText: continuously for at least 2 weeks. Take the cue from the locals, and only skate when you see large numbers of locals doing so. Also, be particularly careful near bridges as the ice tends to be thinner there. If you see the locals avoiding a particular area, you should too.
              [0-2918] region: See
                [0-7743] div
                  [0-2919] heading: See
                  [0-2921] link: edit
                [0-2923] region: Architecture
                  [0-7753] div
                    [0-2924] heading: Architecture
                    [0-2926] link: edit
                  [0-2928] figure
                    [0-2929] link
                      [0-637] image
                    [0-7763] Figcaption
                      [0-2930] StaticText: Idyllic canals and houses with hoists
                  [0-2931] figure
                    [0-2932] link
                      [0-638] image
                    [0-7766] Figcaption
                  [0-2933] paragraph
                    [0-2934] StaticText: Amsterdam has one of the largest
                    [0-2935] StaticText: historic city centres
                    [0-2936] StaticText: in Europe, with about 7,000 registered historic buildings. The street pattern has been largely unchanged since the 19th century—there was no major bombing during World War II. The centre consists of 90 islands linked by 400 bridges, some of them beautifully lit at night.
                  [0-2937] paragraph
                    [0-2938] StaticText: The inner part of the city centre, the
                    [0-2939] link: Binnenstad
                    [0-2941] StaticText: , dates from medieval times. The oldest streets are the Warmoesstraat and the Zeedijk in the
                    [0-2942] StaticText: Oudezijde
                    [0-2943] StaticText: of the Binnenstad. As buildings were made of wood in the Middle Ages, not many of this period's buildings have survived. Two
                    [0-2944] StaticText: medieval wooden houses
                    [0-2945] StaticText: did survive though, at Begijnhof 34 and Zeedijk 1. Other old houses are Warmoesstraat 83 (built around 1400), Warmoesstraat 5 (around 1500) and Begijnhof 2-3 (around 1425). The
                    [0-2946] StaticText: Begijnhof
                    [0-2947] StaticText: is a late-medieval enclosed courtyard with the houses of beguines, Roman Catholic women living in a semi-religious community. Beguines are found in Northern France, Belgium, the Netherlands, and north-western Germany. House number 34 at the Begijnhof is the oldest home in Amsterdam. Entry to the courtyard and surrounding gardens is free, but be careful not to disturb the local community still living here.
                  [0-2948] paragraph
                    [0-2949] StaticText: One of the most prominent features is the
                    [0-2950] link: Canal District
                    [0-2952] StaticText: , a concentric ring of canals built in the 17th century. The merchant-based oligarchy that ruled the trading city of Amsterdam built canal houses and mansions in the most prestigious locations here, especially along the main canals. Typical for the country are its traditional white draw bridges. The best example has to be the
                    [0-2953] StaticText: Magere Brug
                    [0-2954] StaticText: , which is over 300 years old and nearly in its original capacity. It is a beautiful place to overlook the river and take in some traditional Dutch architecture.
                  [0-2955] paragraph
                    [0-2956] StaticText: The
                    [0-2957] link: Jordaan
                    [0-2959] StaticText: was built around 1650 along with the Canal District, but not for the wealthy merchants. For a long time it was considered a typical working-class area, and included some notorious slums. The name probably derives from the nickname 'Jordan' for the Prinsengracht. Apart from a few wider canals, the streets are narrow, in an incomplete grid pattern (as the grid followed the lines of the former polders located here in medieval times). This district is the best example of "gentrification" in the Netherlands, becoming a hip boutique district.
                  [0-2960] paragraph
                    [0-2961] StaticText: There are several
                    [0-2962] StaticText: large warehouses
                    [0-2963] StaticText: for more specific uses. The biggest is the Admiralty Arsenal (1656-1657), now
                    [0-2964] StaticText: Het Scheepvaartmuseum
                    [0-2965] StaticText: at Kattenburgerplein. Others include the former turf warehouses (1550) along the Nes, now the municipal pawn office; a similar warehouse at Waterlooplein 69-75 (Arsenaal, 1610), now an architectural academy, and the warehouse of the West India Company (1642) at the corner of Prins Hendrikkade and 's-Gravenhekje.
                  [0-2966] paragraph
                    [0-2967] StaticText: Windmills
                    [0-2968] StaticText: were not built in urban areas, since the buildings obstructed the wind. The windmills in Amsterdam were all originally outside its city walls. There are a total of eight windmills in the city, most of them in
                    [0-2969] link: West
                    [0-2971] StaticText: . However, the best one to visit is
                    [0-2972] StaticText: De Gooyer
                    [0-2973] StaticText: , which is not far from the city centre, and is being used as a brewery. The only windmill fully open to the public is the
                    [0-2974] StaticText: Molen van Sloten
                    [0-2975] StaticText: in Sloten, a former village now part of
                    [0-2976] link: West
                    [0-2978] StaticText: .
                [0-2979] region: Museums
                  [0-7778] div
                    [0-2980] heading: Museums
                    [0-2982] link: edit
                  [0-2984] figure
                    [0-2985] link
                      [0-631] image
                    [0-7789] Figcaption
                      [0-2986] StaticText: Rijksmuseum
                  [0-2987] paragraph
                    [0-2988] StaticText: Amsterdam has an amazing collection of museums. The most popular ones can get
                    [0-2989] StaticText: very
                    [0-2990] StaticText: crowded in the summer peak season, so it's worth exploring advance tickets or getting there off-peak (e.g. very early in the morning). Avoid the museums in the
                    [0-2991] link: Binnenstad
                    [0-2993] StaticText: as these are mostly tourist traps. The quality museums can be found in
                    [0-2994] link: Zuid
                    [0-2996] StaticText: , the
                    [0-647] link: Canal District
                    [0-2998] StaticText: and
                    [0-2999] link: Plantage
                    [0-3001] StaticText: . The museums in Zuid are located at the
                    [0-3002] StaticText: Museumplein
                    [0-3003] StaticText: , a square surrounded by quality museums. The country's national museum is the
                    [0-3004] StaticText: Rijksmuseum
                    [0-3005] StaticText: , a must-visit with a large collection of paintings from the Dutch Golden Age. Some artists that can't be overlooked are Rembrandt, Johannes Vermeer, Frans Hals and Jan Steen. The most widely regarded paintings are Rembrandt's
                    [0-3006] StaticText: Night Watch
                    [0-3007] StaticText: and Vermeer's
                    [0-3008] StaticText: Milkmaid
                    [0-3009] StaticText: . The museum also boasts a substantial collection of Asian art. Reopened after a reconstruction of about ten years, its renewed set-up is absolutely worthwhile, leading the visitor through the ages from the late Middle Ages to the early 20th century.
                  [0-3010] paragraph
                    [0-3011] StaticText: Even someone with little knowledge of art must have heard about Vincent van Gogh, the Dutch Post-Impressionist painter whose work had a far-reaching influence on 20th century art for its vivid colours and emotional impact. The
                    [0-3012] StaticText: Van Gogh Museum
                    [0-3013] StaticText: has the largest collection of Van Gogh's paintings and drawings in the world. The
                    [0-3014] StaticText: Stedelijk Museum
                    [0-3015] StaticText: is all about modern art, contemporary art and design. A newer addition to Amsterdam's already stellar set of art museums is the
                    [0-3016] StaticText: H'ART Museum
                    [0-3017] StaticText: in
                    [0-3018] link: Plantage
                    [0-3020] StaticText: which has affiliations with Centre Pompidou, British Museum and Smithsonian American Art Museum.
                  [0-3021] paragraph
                    [0-3022] StaticText: A major museum is the
                    [0-3023] StaticText: Anne Frank House
                    [0-3024] StaticText: , dedicated to Anne Frank, a Jewish girl who kept a diary while hiding from Nazi persecution in hidden rooms at the rear of a building in the
                    [0-3025] link: Canal District
                    [0-3027] StaticText: (known as the
                    [0-3028] StaticText: Achterhuis
                    [0-3029] StaticText: ). It's an exhibition on the life of Anne Frank, but also highlights other forms of persecution and discrimination. Amsterdam has hundreds of museums about pretty much every topic one could think of. They are described in the city's district articles.
                  [0-3030] paragraph
                    [0-3031] StaticText: The
                    [0-3032] link: Museumkaart
                    [0-3034] StaticText: costs
                    [0-7802] Abbr: €75.00 ≈ US$86, UK£65, CA$122, AU$123, NZ$150
                      [0-3035] StaticText: €75.00
                    [0-3036] StaticText: for adults and
                    [0-7803] Abbr: €39.00 ≈ US$44.7, UK£33.8, CA$63.3, AU$63.8, NZ$77.9
                      [0-3037] StaticText: €39.00
                    [0-3038] StaticText: for those under 18 years old (2025). It covers the cost of admission to over 500 museums across the Netherlands and you can buy it at most major museums. You can opt for a digital or a physical card. Note that if you choose for the latter one and do not buy it in advance, you will be issued a temporary card that is only valid for 5 museum visits over a period of 31 days until you receive the permanent card, which can be mailed to a EU address after being registered. It is valid for an entire year. If you are going to the Rijksmuseum and Van Gogh Museum, those are
                    [0-7804] Abbr: €25.00 ≈ US$28.7, UK£21.7, CA$40.6, AU$40.9, NZ$49.9
                      [0-3039] StaticText: €25.00
                    [0-3040] StaticText: and
                    [0-7805] Abbr: €24.00 ≈ US$27.5, UK£20.8, CA$38.9, AU$39.2, NZ$47.9
                      [0-3041] StaticText: €24.00
                    [0-3042] StaticText: (2025) respectively, so this card can quickly pay for itself. The tickets to the major museums, including the audio guide, can be bought early from the tourist information desk at no extra cost. Alternatively, for short stays, you can consider buying the
                    [0-3043] link: I amsterdam City Card
                    [0-3045] StaticText: , starting at
                    [0-7807] Abbr: €65 ≈ US$74.5, UK£56.3, CA$105, AU$106, NZ$130
                      [0-3046] StaticText: €65
                    [0-3047] StaticText: (2025) per day, which includes "free" access to Amsterdam museums, public transport and discounts on many tourist attractions.
                [0-3048] region: Churches and synagogues
                  [0-7808] div
                    [0-3049] heading: Churches and synagogues
                    [0-3051] link: edit
                  [0-3053] paragraph
                    [0-3054] StaticText: Since the Middle Ages, the Netherlands has been a country with a relatively high degree of freedom and tolerance towards other religions and cultures, especially compared to other countries in Europe, with the major exception being the persecution of Catholics after winning the war with Spain and during and after the Eighty Years' War.  Between 1590 and 1800, the estimated foreign-born population was never less than 5 percent, many of them settling in Amsterdam. This led to a large migration of Jews, Huguenots (French Protestants), Flemings, Poles and other people to the city. Jews in particular had a large presence in Amsterdam, notably in the
                    [0-3055] link: Jodenbuurt
                    [0-3057] StaticText: , though this quarter has changed significantly after World War II. The most prominent synagogue is
                    [0-3058] StaticText: The Esnoga
                    [0-3059] StaticText: (or
                    [0-3060] StaticText: The Portuguese Synagogue
                    [0-3061] StaticText: ), built in 1675 in an austere Classicist style.
                  [0-3062] paragraph
                    [0-3063] StaticText: As the Netherlands was a Protestant nation, most of the churches are from this branch of Christianity. The oldest church in Amsterdam, the Netherlands-gothic
                    [0-3064] StaticText: Oude Kerk
                    [0-3065] StaticText: on the Oudezijds Voorburgwal at Oudekerksplein, is now surrounded by window prostitution. It was built in 1306, and became a Calvinist church after the Reformation in 1578. The
                    [0-3066] StaticText: Nieuwe Kerk
                    [0-3067] StaticText: , at Dam Square, dates from the 15th century and is now used for royal coronations and exhibitions. From the 17th century onwards, four compass churches were built that would serve the areas outside the Binnenstad.
                  [0-3068] paragraph
                    [0-3069] StaticText: The late-medieval city also had smaller chapels such as the Sint Olofskapel (circa 1440) on Zeedijk, and convent chapels such as the Agnietenkapel on the Oudezijds Voorburgwal 231 (originally 1470), now the University of Amsterdam museum. Later churches included the Oosterkerk (1669) in the eastern islands, and the heavily restored Lutheran Church on the Singel (1671), now used by a hotel as a conference centre. Catholic churches were long forbidden, and built again only in the 19th-century. The most prominent is the Neo-Baroque Church of St. Nicholas (1887) opposite Centraal Station. Also, investigate some of the "hidden churches" found in Amsterdam, mainly Catholic churches that remained in activity following the Reformation. A prominent hidden church is
                    [0-3070] StaticText: Ons' Lieve Heer op Solder
                    [0-3071] StaticText: . Well worth the visit. Two hidden churches still in use are the Begijnhofchapel near the Spui, and the Papegaaikerk in the Kalverstraat (both Catholic).
                [0-3072] region: Modern architecture
                  [0-7822] div
                    [0-3073] heading: Modern architecture
                    [0-3075] link: edit
                  [0-3077] figure
                    [0-3078] link
                      [0-629] image
                    [0-7832] Figcaption
                      [0-3079] StaticText: "Het Schip", Amsterdam School architecture in the Zaanstraat
                  [0-3080] paragraph
                    [0-3081] StaticText: Since there was little large-scale demolition in the historic city centre, most modern architecture is outside of it. Immediately outside the Singelgracht (the former city moat) is a ring of 19th century housing. The most prominent buildings from this period are the Amsterdam Centraal railway station (1889) and the Rijksmuseum (1885), both by Pierre Cuypers.
                    [0-3082] link: De Pijp
                    [0-3084] StaticText: is a textbook example of 19th century revolution-build, cheap construction housing. The most prominent in architectural history are the residential complexes by architects of the
                    [0-3085] StaticText: Amsterdam School
                    [0-3086] StaticText: , for instance at Zaanstraat and Oostzaanstraat in
                    [0-3087] link: West
                    [0-3089] StaticText: . The Amsterdam School is a style of Expressionist architecture that arose from 1910 through about 1930. Examples can be found in De Baarsjes in
                    [0-3090] link: West
                    [0-3092] StaticText: and the Rivierenbuurt in
                    [0-3093] link: Zuid
                    [0-3095] StaticText: .
                  [0-3096] paragraph
                    [0-3097] StaticText: A completely different approach to architecture has been followed in the
                    [0-645] link: Bijlmer
                    [0-3099] StaticText: , a huge architectural project undertaken in the 1970s. A series of nearly identical high-rise buildings were laid out in a hexagonal grid with a strict separation of pedestrian and car traffic. It has been a revolutionary way of thinking in the architectural world, but within a decade the district started to make headlines with crime and robberies. As these high-rises are being torn down, the safety situation has improved, and now modern office buildings are taking their place.
                  [0-3100] paragraph
                    [0-3101] StaticText: The 1990s and 2000s also left its mark as a revolutionary time in architectural design. The
                    [0-3102] StaticText: Eastern Docklands
                    [0-3103] StaticText: is the largest concentration of modern residential buildings. The zone includes three artificial islands: Borneo, Sporenburg, and KNSM/Java-eiland. The latter has been designed as a modern re-imagining of the old Canal District. Across from it is the brand new Piet Heinkade and some adjoining projects. The largest concentration of box-like office buildings is in the
                    [0-3104] link: Zuidas
                    [0-3106] StaticText: and in
                    [0-3107] link: Zuidoost
                    [0-3109] StaticText: . Some spectacular buildings are Johan Cruijff ArenA (formerly Amsterdam ArenA) stadium and the new Bijlmer ArenA railway station.
              [0-3110] region: Do
                [0-7836] div
                  [0-3111] heading: Do
                  [0-3113] link: edit
                [0-3115] paragraph
                  [0-3116] StaticText: The locals spend their summer days in Amsterdam uncorking bottles of red wine in the
                  [0-3117] StaticText: Vondelpark
                  [0-3118] StaticText: . Every district in Amsterdam has at least one park, but the
                  [0-3119] link: Vondelpark
                  [0-3121] StaticText: stands out for its size and convivial atmosphere. The neighbourhood best known for its trees and gardens is the
                  [0-3122] link: Plantage
                  [0-3124] StaticText: . Besides leafy boulevards and grand mansions it also features the botanical gardens of the
                  [0-3125] StaticText: Hortus Botanicus
                  [0-3126] StaticText: and has
                  [0-3127] StaticText: Artis Zoo
                  [0-3128] StaticText: for the kids.
                [0-3129] paragraph
                  [0-3130] StaticText: Another major patch of nature is
                  [0-3131] StaticText: Amsterdamse Bos
                  [0-3132] StaticText: , which, directly translated, means Amsterdam Forest, but is more like a giant park. Amsterdamse Bos also offers Fun Forest, a climbing trail between the trees, and the Bosmuseum about the forest, which is actually a lot of fun, especially if you're
                  [0-3133] link: travelling with children
                  [0-3135] StaticText: . Both are near the main entrance in Amsterdam Zuid. Amsterdamse Bos is on the outskirts of the city, not far from Schiphol, partially in
                  [0-3136] link: Amstelveen
                  [0-3138] StaticText: and Ouderkerk, and near
                  [0-3139] link: Aalsmeer
                  [0-3141] StaticText: Nieuw Oosteinde.
                [0-3142] paragraph
                  [0-3143] StaticText: Amsterdam also has several
                  [0-3144] StaticText: city beaches
                  [0-3145] StaticText: in
                  [0-3146] link: West
                  [0-3148] StaticText: (Zwemstrand Sloterplas),
                  [0-3149] link: Noord
                  [0-3151] StaticText: (Pllek),
                  [0-3152] link: Oost
                  [0-3154] StaticText: (Kaap and Strand IJburg),
                  [0-3155] link: Zuid
                  [0-3157] StaticText: (Strandzuid) and
                  [0-3158] link: Zuidoost
                  [0-3160] StaticText: (Gaasperplas).
                [0-3161] paragraph
                  [0-3162] StaticText: You can also watch a film at one of the more than 55
                  [0-3163] StaticText: cinemas
                  [0-3164] StaticText: . Rialto in
                  [0-3165] link: Zuid
                  [0-3167] StaticText: and Kriterion in
                  [0-3168] link: Plantage
                  [0-3170] StaticText: run a selection of art house and alternative films, and LAB111 in West often shows cult movies. The EYE Film Institute in
                  [0-3171] link: Noord
                  [0-3173] StaticText: is dedicated to film conservation, but also has screenings and exhibitions.
                [0-3174] paragraph
                  [0-3175] StaticText: Football:
                  [0-9507] StaticText: 
                  [0-3176] link: AFC Ajax
                  [0-3178] StaticText: play soccer in Eredivisie, the Dutch top tier, and often win it. Their home ground is Johan Cruijff ArenA (capacity 56,120) 5 km south of the centre, metro and train station Bijlmer ArenA, which also hosts internationals. Their second-string team Jong Ajax (or "Ajax 2") plays in Eerste Divisie, the second tier, at Sportpark De Toekomst near the ArenA.

                    [0-3188] StaticText: A
                    [0-3189] StaticText: canal cruise
                    [0-3190] StaticText: usually lasts from one to two hours. Commentary on the surroundings is given during the route.
