              [0-3770] region: Work
                [0-8554] div
                  [0-3771] heading: Work
                  [0-3773] link: edit
                [0-3775] paragraph
                  [0-3776] StaticText: Many people will find it difficult to get a suitable job if they do not speak Dutch. However, hostels and hotels in Amsterdam may need bar staff, night porters etc., who speak English and other languages. There are also specialist websites for English and non-Dutch speakers looking to work in Amsterdam and they are often a good place to start.
                [0-3777] paragraph
                  [0-3778] StaticText: Immigration matters are dealt with by the immigration service
                  [0-3779] link: IND
                  [0-3781] StaticText: . Registration is done by both police and municipalities. Immigration policy is restrictive and deliberately bureaucratic, this is especially true for non-EU citizens.
                [0-3782] paragraph
                  [0-3783] StaticText: European Union citizens do not require a work permit. Australians, New Zealanders and Canadians are afforded a one-year working-holiday visa. In general the
                  [0-3784] StaticText: employer
                  [0-3785] StaticText: must apply for work permits. Immigration is easier for higher educated (Bachelor's or higher) earning a gross annual salary of over
                  [0-8564] Abbr: €45000 ≈ US$51600, UK£39000, CA$73000, AU$73600, NZ$89900
                    [0-3786] StaticText: €45000
                  [0-3787] StaticText: (over
                  [0-8565] Abbr: €33000 ≈ US$37800, UK£28600, CA$53600, AU$53900, NZ$65900
                    [0-3788] StaticText: €33000
                  [0-3789] StaticText: for those under 30).
              [0-3790] region: Buy
                [0-8566] div
                  [0-3791] heading: Buy
                  [0-3793] link: edit
                [0-3795] DescriptionList
                  [0-3796] definition
                    [0-3797] StaticText: Individual listings can be found in Amsterdam's
                    [0-3798] link: district
                    [0-3800] StaticText: articles
                [0-3801] figure
                  [0-3802] link
                    [0-633] image
                  [0-8578] Figcaption
                    [0-3803] StaticText: Tulips from Amsterdam
                [0-3804] paragraph
                  [0-3805] StaticText: The main
                  [0-3806] StaticText: central shopping streets
                  [0-3807] StaticText: run in a line from Centraal Station to the Leidseplein: Nieuwendijk, Kalverstraat, Heiligeweg, Leidsestraat. The emphasis is on clothing and fashion, but there are plenty of other shops. These are not upmarket shopping streets, and the north end of Nieuwendijk is a bit seedy. English-language books can be found in the shops around
                  [0-3808] StaticText: Spui
                  [0-3809] StaticText: , and a used book market is held there every Friday. There is a concentration of Chinese shops in Zeedijk and Nieuwmarkt, and flowers can be bought at the
                  [0-3810] StaticText: Bloemenmarkt
                  [0-3811] StaticText: . However, do not buy bulbs there. They are usually too old to have even a slight chance of growing. Other concentrations of shops in the centre are Utrechtsestraat, Spiegelstraat (art and antiques) and Staalstraat (specialty shops).
                [0-3812] paragraph
                  [0-3813] StaticText: Interesting independent shops and boutiques are located in the side streets of the main canals (Prinsengracht, Keizersgracht, Herengracht) and especially in the
                  [0-3814] link: Jordaan
                  [0-3816] StaticText: . The
                  [0-3817] StaticText: Haarlemmerstraat
                  [0-3818] StaticText: and Haarlemmerdijk are claimed as best shopping streets in the Netherlands. The area around Museumplein in
                  [0-3819] link: Zuid
                  [0-3821] StaticText: has Amsterdam's upmarket shopping streets. The
                  [0-3822] StaticText: P.C. Hooftstraat
                  [0-3823] StaticText: and the
                  [0-3824] StaticText: Cornelis Schuytstraat
                  [0-3825] StaticText: have the finest designer shops in the city. You can find designer shoes, health and well-being specialists, massage parlors, fashion boutiques, designer interiors, designer florists and specialist shops. The partly gentrified neighbourhood of De Pijp—around Ferdinand Bolstraat and Sarphatipark—is slowly becoming the 'second Jordaan'.
                [0-3826] paragraph
                  [0-3827] StaticText: Street markets originally sold mainly food, and most still sell food and clothing, but they have become more specialized. The
                  [0-3828] StaticText: Albert Cuyp Market
                  [0-3829] StaticText: is the largest in Amsterdam, and the best-known street market in the country. The
                  [0-3830] StaticText: Waterloopleinmarkt
                  [0-3831] StaticText: is partly a flea market, partly an alternative and second hand clothing and accessories market. It is more oriented towards tourists than to locals. If you're looking for authenticity, visit the
                  [0-3832] StaticText: Dappermarkt
                  [0-3833] StaticText: in
                  [0-3834] link: Oost
                  [0-3836] StaticText: or the
                  [0-3837] StaticText: Ten Katemarkt
                  [0-3838] StaticText: in
                  [0-3839] link: West
                  [0-3841] StaticText: . Both have food, households, flowers and clothing, and have a multicultural flavor.
                [0-3842] paragraph
                  [0-3843] StaticText: In the areas surrounding the city centre, the main shopping streets are the Kinkerstraat, Ferdinand Bolstraat, Van Woustraat, and the Javastraat. The most ethnically diverse shopping street in Amsterdam is the
                  [0-3844] StaticText: Javastraat
                  [0-3845] StaticText: . There are some toy stores and clothing shops for
                  [0-3846] StaticText: kids
                  [0-3847] StaticText: in the centre, but most are in the shopping streets further out, because that's where families with children live. Particularly
                  [0-3848] link: IJburg
                  [0-3850] StaticText: has a good set of shops for families.
              [0-3851] region: Eat
                [0-8592] div
                  [0-3852] heading: Eat
                  [0-3854] link: edit
                [0-3856] DescriptionList
                  [0-3857] definition
                    [0-3858] StaticText: Individual listings can be found in Amsterdam's
                    [0-3859] link: district
                    [0-3861] StaticText: articles
                [0-3862] figure
                  [0-3863] link
                    [0-636] image
                  [0-8604] Figcaption
                    [0-3864] StaticText: Bitterballen with mustard
                [0-3865] paragraph
                  [0-3866] StaticText: Amsterdam's culinary scene boasts a vibrant tapestry of flavours, offering a rich variety of dining experiences. The city unfolds as a treasure trove for those craving Asian cuisine, albeit catered to the milder local palate. Adventurous taste buds, fear not – it's not impossible to find spicy food.
                [0-3867] paragraph
                  [0-3868] StaticText: Most noticeably, a legacy of Dutch colonial history is woven into the dining fabric, evident through the profusion of Indonesian and Surinamese restaurants. Like other cities filled with tourists, Amsterdam's true culinary scene can be found along the quieter byways, where value and authenticity often intermingle away from the bustling tourist centres.
                [0-3869] paragraph
                  [0-3870] StaticText: The Lange Leidsedwarsstraat (just off Leidseplein) has about five Italian restaurants that sell pasta or pizza for
                  [0-8606] Abbr: €5 ≈ US$5.7, UK£4.3, CA$8.1, AU$8.2, NZ$10
                    [0-3871] StaticText: €5
                  [0-3872] StaticText: among many tourist traps. Many restaurants of all kinds can be found in the
                  [0-3873] link: Haarlemmerbuurt
                  [0-3875] StaticText: . Also worth trying is the Van Woustraat in
                  [0-3876] link: De Pijp
                  [0-3878] StaticText: , or continue to the Rijnstraat in the
                  [0-3879] link: Rivierenbuurt
                  [0-3881] StaticText: . Exquisite but expensive restaurants can be found in the
                  [0-3882] link: Utrechtsestraat
                  [0-3884] StaticText: . While there are exceptions, in general avoid restaurants along Damrak and be cautious around Leidseplein—they are well known tourist traps.
                [0-3885] region: Asian cuisine
                  [0-8607] div
                    [0-3886] heading: Asian cuisine
                    [0-3888] link: edit
                  [0-3890] paragraph
                    [0-3891] StaticText: Amsterdam's de facto Chinatown is at
                    [0-3892] StaticText: Zeedijk
                    [0-3893] StaticText: , near the bustling
                    [0-3894] link: Nieuwmarkt
                    [0-3896] StaticText: square, where you can find a delightful array of Asian eateries, not limited to Chinese, Thai and Japanese restaurants. It contains many
                    [0-3897] StaticText: tokos
                    [0-3898] StaticText: , which are small East Asian grocery stores containing Eastern culinary treasures and aromatic spices. Chinatown also contains Indonesian and Indian restaurants, though the latter can get expensive, depending on your budget.
                  [0-3899] paragraph
                    [0-3900] StaticText: Budget-friendly feasts can be found along the charming lanes of
                    [0-3901] StaticText: Damstraat
                    [0-3902] StaticText: and
                    [0-3903] StaticText: Muntplein
                    [0-3904] StaticText: , where many Middle Eastern establishments can be found.
                [0-3905] region: Surinamese cuisine
                  [0-8621] div
                    [0-3906] heading: Surinamese cuisine
                    [0-3908] link: edit
                  [0-3910] paragraph
                    [0-3911] StaticText: Amsterdam may not be your first thought when it comes to Surinamese cuisine, but nobody said you couldn't savour this relatively-unknown culinary delight. The best places to find Surinamese cuisine are
                    [0-3912] link: Zuid
                    [0-3914] StaticText: and Zuidoost, especially along the eminent
                    [0-3915] StaticText: Albert Cuypstraat
                    [0-3916] StaticText: . Local favourites include
                    [0-3917] StaticText: roti met bonen
                    [0-3918] StaticText: ,
                    [0-3919] StaticText: moksi meti
                    [0-3920] StaticText: ,
                    [0-3921] StaticText: petjil
                    [0-3922] StaticText: , and the sweet finale of
                    [0-3923] StaticText: bojo
                    [0-3924] StaticText: as a dessert.
                  [0-3925] paragraph
                    [0-3926] StaticText: A popular drink that you can't not try is
                    [0-3927] StaticText: dawet
                    [0-3928] StaticText: – it's a unique beverage crafted from milk, coconut and rose syrup, featuring delightful sago balls (kids also ostensibly like it). Although popularised in Suriname, its origins trace back to Indonesia – as such, you can find it in several Indonesian restaurants.
                [0-3929] region: Local specialities
                  [0-8636] div
                    [0-3930] heading: Local specialities
                    [0-3932] link: edit
                  [0-3934] paragraph
                    [0-3935] StaticText: Cheese
                    [0-3936] StaticText: can be bought at the Albert Cuyp Market, or at specialist cheese shops found around the city centre. Dutch cheese is traditionally firm, made in large wax-covered wheels, and falls into two main categories—young and old. There is a rich variety within these categories. Among the more unusual young cheeses is cumin cheese (
                    [0-3937] StaticText: komijnenkaas
                    [0-3938] StaticText: ), which is particular to the Netherlands. Sheep cheese (
                    [0-3939] StaticText: schapenkaas
                    [0-3940] StaticText: ) and goat cheese (
                    [0-3941] StaticText: geitenkaas
                    [0-3942] StaticText: ) are also common. Old cheese can be made of any sort of milk, and is often reminiscent of Italian Parmesan in consistency and sharpness of flavour.
                  [0-3943] paragraph
                    [0-3944] StaticText: Check out
                    [0-3945] StaticText: bitterballen
                    [0-3946] StaticText: , fried breaded ragout balls, and
                    [0-3947] StaticText: kroketten
                    [0-3948] StaticText: (the same, but shaped like a cylinder), but take care not to burn your mouth. Also don't forget to try a
                    [0-3949] StaticText: traditional herring
                    [0-3950] StaticText: or a
                    [0-3951] StaticText: broodje haring
                    [0-3952] StaticText: (herring sandwich), available from fish stalls around the city. Herring in Amsterdam is usually served with onions and pickles. A good try is the fish stand on the Koningsplein near the Bloemenmarkt.
                    [0-3953] StaticText: Syrup waffles
                    [0-3954] StaticText: (
                    [0-3955] StaticText: stroopwafels
                    [0-3956] StaticText: ) are made fresh at the Albert Cuyp. If you're visiting in late November or December, you can enjoy
                    [0-3957] StaticText: oliebollen
                    [0-3958] StaticText: , which are round blobs of sweet fried dough available with or without raisins (sultanas) embedded and dusted with powdered sugar.
              [0-3959] region: Drink
                [0-8656] div
                  [0-3960] heading: Drink
                  [0-3962] link: edit
                [0-3964] DescriptionList
                  [0-3965] definition
                    [0-3966] StaticText: Individual listings can be found in Amsterdam's
                    [0-3967] link: district
                    [0-3969] StaticText: articles
                [0-3970] figure
                  [0-3971] link
                    [0-634] image
                  [0-8668] Figcaption
                    [0-3972] StaticText: Bruin café
                    [0-3973] StaticText: in Amsterdam
                [0-3974] paragraph
                  [0-3975] StaticText: Amsterdam's famously wild nightlife caters to all tastes and budgets. The archetypical Amsterdam watering hole is the
                  [0-3976] StaticText: bruine café
                  [0-3977] StaticText: ("brown bar"), a neighbourhood bar of sorts with gorgeous dark wood panelling—hence the name—and booths.
                  [0-3978] StaticText: Grand cafés
                  [0-3979] StaticText: are more grand and spacious, and also serve small food portions. These usually have at least one long table with newspapers and magazines. Lounge and designer bars pop up across the city catering to the city's younger and more trend susceptible crowd. If you're a beer lover consider visiting a beer shop or tasting room in the
                  [0-3980] link: Binnenstad
                  [0-3982] StaticText: or the brewery in
                  [0-3983] link: Plantage
                  [0-3985] StaticText: . There are some excellent beers you can get from this part of the world such as wheat beer (
                  [0-3986] StaticText: witbeer
                  [0-3987] StaticText: ).
                [0-3988] paragraph
                  [0-3989] StaticText: The nightclubs in Amsterdam are not as rough as one might think. Many of them congregate around
                  [0-3990] StaticText: Leidseplein
                  [0-3991] StaticText: and
                  [0-3992] StaticText: Rembrandtplein
                  [0-3993] StaticText: in the
                  [0-3994] link: Canal District
                  [0-3996] StaticText: . You can't go wrong at
                  [0-3997] StaticText: Melkweg
                  [0-3998] StaticText: ,
                  [0-3999] StaticText: Sugar Factory
                  [0-4000] StaticText: and
                  [0-4001] StaticText: Paradiso
                  [0-4002] StaticText: , three live music venues that usually have large queues on weekends. Paradiso has the best interior, as it used to be a church, while Melkweg feels more like a nightclub. Sugar Factory is a little more intimate and is a multidisciplinary platform for young talent.
                  [0-4003] StaticText: Jimmy Woo
                  [0-4004] StaticText: is an impressive VIP-room, and a strict dress code applies. There are also some nightclubs in
                  [0-4005] link: Oost
                  [0-4007] StaticText: , such as
                  [0-4008] StaticText: Panama
                  [0-4009] StaticText: , and near the
                  [0-4010] link: Westerpark
                  [0-4012] StaticText: . Amsterdam's
                  [0-4013] StaticText: gay nightlife
                  [0-4014] StaticText: is not as vibrant it used to be, but there is still an active community in the
                  [0-4015] StaticText: Reguliersdwarsstraat
                  [0-4016] StaticText: in the
                  [0-4017] link: Canal District
                  [0-4019] StaticText: . The annual
                  [0-4020] StaticText: gay pride
                  [0-4021] StaticText: in August is a fun event that can be attended by gays and straights alike.
                [0-4022] region: Coffeeshops
                  [0-8684] div
                    [0-4023] heading: Coffeeshops
                    [0-4025] link: edit
                  [0-4027] figure
                    [0-4028] link
                      [0-627] image
                    [0-8694] Figcaption
                      [0-4029] StaticText: "Hash brownies", cakes containing hashish, purchased at three different Amsterdam coffeeshops in 2007
                  [0-4030] paragraph
                    [0-4031] StaticText: Amsterdam is renowned for its liberal
                    [0-4032] StaticText: drug policy
                    [0-4033] StaticText: . Coffeeshops (in English, but written as one word; not to be confused with coffeehouses or cafés) are allowed to sell
                    [0-4034] StaticText: cannabis
                    [0-4035] StaticText: and hash for personal use, i.e. not more than 5
                    [0-4036] StaticText: 
                    [0-4037] StaticText: grams. While still illegal, mostly to comply with international treaties, personal use of soft drugs is regulated by the Ministry of Justice under an official policy of
                    [0-4038] StaticText: gedogen
                    [0-4039] StaticText: . Literally this means
                    [0-4040] StaticText: to accept
                    [0-4041] StaticText: or
                    [0-4042] StaticText: tolerate
                    [0-4043] StaticText: ; legally it is a doctrine of non-prosecution on the basis that action taken would be so highly irregular as to constitute selective prosecution. The city council of Amsterdam allows coffeeshops to operate only with the provision of set, non-transferable licenses as shown by an official green and white sticker on the window of a coffeeshop. Coffeeshops are to sell only soft drugs such as cannabis, selling of other drugs is not allowed. Also selling of dried hallucinogenic mushrooms is not allowed.
                  [0-4044] paragraph
                    [0-4045] StaticText: There are about 250 coffeeshops in Amsterdam, most of them in the
                    [0-4046] link: Binnenstad
                    [0-4048] StaticText: . Marijuana is mostly sold in one-gram increments with a maximum limit of 5
                    [0-4049] StaticText: 
                    [0-4050] StaticText: grams per transaction. Prices hover around
                    [0-8703] Abbr: €10 ≈ US$11, UK£8.7, CA$16, AU$16, NZ$20
                      [0-4051] StaticText: €10
                    [0-4052] StaticText: for 1
                    [0-4053] StaticText: 
                    [0-4054] StaticText: gram, with the average joint holding around 0.33g. Most coffeeshops are happy to recommend varieties and prepare your joint for you. Some offer vaporizers/inhalers for people who don't want to smoke. Smoking paraphernalia is usually available upon request. It is common practice not to smoke at a coffeeshop without purchasing something from the establishment first, be it coffee, a Coke, or marijuana. All coffeeshops do, indeed, sell coffee as well. ID is requested upon entrance to each establishment, and more often than not the only acceptable ID is a passport.
                  [0-4055] paragraph
                    [0-4056] StaticText: Many coffeeshops offer a 'smoking lounge' where soft drugs may be used. Despite the confusion on the subject, the country-wide smoking ban applies only to tobacco. However, since the Dutch commonly smoke tobacco mixed with their marijuana or hash, many coffeeshops, especially those unaccustomed to tourists, may require all smoking to be done in a separated smoking section or outdoors. Most central coffeeshops with large tourist clientèles will allow marijuana or hash smoking in their entire space, requiring you to smoke in the separated section only if your joint contains tobacco. Many coffeeshops also provide a non-tobacco herbal filler for those who find pure joints too strong. You may usually smoke joints containing this herbal filler anywhere within the coffeeshop although individual house rules may vary. If in doubt, always ask the staff.
                  [0-4057] paragraph
                    [0-4058] StaticText: Amsterdam hosts the Cannabis Cup, the most important marijuana related event in the world every year during the week of Thanksgiving. The Cannabis Cup is organized by
                    [0-4059] StaticText: High Times
                    [0-4060] StaticText: magazine, and offers both tourists and natives the chance to enjoy 5 days of consuming and judging marijuana in different forms. Participants are eligible to pay $199 in advance or
                    [0-8706] Abbr: €250 ≈ US$287, UK£217, CA$406, AU$409, NZ$499
                      [0-4061] StaticText: €250
                    [0-4062] StaticText: at the door to obtain a "judges pass", which allows entry to the event for all five days, admission to numerous concerts and seminars held during the event, the ability to vote on numerous awards that are handed out, and free bus tours to and from the event. Day passes are available for
                    [0-8707] Abbr: €30 ≈ US$34, UK£26, CA$49, AU$49, NZ$60
                      [0-4063] StaticText: €30
                    [0-4064] StaticText: for each day, and certain concerts sell tickets at the door provided they are not already sold out.
                [0-4065] region: Red Light District
                  [0-8708] div
                    [0-4066] heading: Red Light District
                    [0-4068] link: edit
                  [0-4070] paragraph
                    [0-4071] StaticText: The Red Light District consists of several canals, and the side streets between them, south of Centraal Station and east of Damrak. It is known as
                    [0-4072] StaticText: De Wallen
                    [0-4073] StaticText: (the quays) in Dutch, because the canals were once part of the city defences (walls and moats). Prostitution itself is limited to certain streets, mainly side streets and alleys, but the district is considered to include the canals, and some adjoining streets. The smell inside can be nauseating especially if you detest the smell of cannabis or even tobacco - keep in mind especially if you're with a group, as it can be very difficult even with a mask on (pre-COVID, at least).
                  [0-4074] paragraph
                    [0-4075] StaticText: The area has many sex shops and peep show bars and is a common attraction for bachelors celebrating a stag night, both of which have become an eye-sore for most locals; if you ever get hassled, a firm and loud "leave me alone" will work most of the time. The whole area has a heavy police presence and many security cameras. Nevertheless, it is still a residential district and has many bars and restaurants, and also includes historic buildings and museums.

                  [0-4107] definition
                    [0-4108] StaticText: Individual listings can be found in Amsterdam's

                [0-4112] paragraph
                  [0-4113] StaticText: Amsterdam has over 400 registered hotels of varying standards from budget facilities to some of the most expensive hotels in Europe. Advance booking is recommended, especially for weekends and holidays. Don't expect you'll find an affordable bed once you're here. Most hotels and hostels can be found in the
                  [0-4114] link: Binnenstad
                  [0-4116] StaticText: , notably south of Centraal Station, and in
                  [0-4117] link: Zuid
                  [0-4119] StaticText: around the Museum Quarter. Charming boutique accommodation can be found in the wealthy residential
                  [0-4120] link: Canal District
                  [0-4122] StaticText: , home to the rich and famous and its squares are the prime nightlife spots of the city. The
                  [0-4123] link: Jordaan
                  [0-4125] StaticText: is another area for hip boutique accommodations, slightly upmarket, but still for mid-range prices. Some cheaper hostels can also be found in the
                  [0-4126] link: Red Light District
                  [0-4128] StaticText: .
                [0-4129] paragraph
                  [0-4130] StaticText: A simple bed in a
                  [0-4131] link: hostel
                  [0-4133] StaticText: starts around
                  [0-8741] Abbr: €18 ≈ US$20.6, UK£15.6, CA$29.2, AU$29.4, NZ$35.9
                    [0-4134] StaticText: €18
                  [0-4135] StaticText: on weekdays in the winter and up to
                  [0-8742] Abbr: €90 ≈ US$100, UK£78, CA$150, AU$150, NZ$180
                    [0-4136] StaticText: €90
                  [0-4137] StaticText: on a weekend in the summer. Hostels often expect you to book at least 2 nights in a weekend. A twin room in a budget hotel, 1-2 stars, might cost around
                  [0-8743] Abbr: €40 ≈ US$46, UK£35, CA$65, AU$65, NZ$80
                    [0-4138] StaticText: €40
                  [0-4139] StaticText: on weekdays in the winter and up to
                  [0-8744] Abbr: €100 ≈ US$110, UK£87, CA$160, AU$160, NZ$200
                    [0-4140] StaticText: €100
                  [0-4141] StaticText: on summer weekends. In a three and four-star hotel, the prices would range from
                  [0-8745] Abbr: €100 ≈ US$110, UK£87, CA$160, AU$160, NZ$200
                    [0-4142] StaticText: €100
                  [0-4143] StaticText: to
                  [0-8746] Abbr: €200 ≈ US$230, UK£170, CA$320, AU$330, NZ$400
                    [0-4144] StaticText: €200
                  [0-4145] StaticText: , depending on season, and five-star hotels can cost between
                  [0-8747] Abbr: €150 ≈ US$172, UK£130, CA$243, AU$245, NZ$300
                    [0-4146] StaticText: €150
                  [0-4147] StaticText: and
                  [0-8748] Abbr: €400 ≈ US$460, UK£350, CA$650, AU$650, NZ$800
                    [0-4148] StaticText: €400
                  [0-4149] StaticText: a night. As a rule of thumb, summer is high season and price can be double compared to winter times. September and October tend to be cheaper months to travel.
                [0-4150] paragraph
                  [0-4151] StaticText: Do not expect a wide number of services from cheaper end hostels and hotels. Most of these do not have elevators and have the usual steep staircases; if you suffer from vertigo, do get an assurance that you will be getting a first or second floor room or book a hotel that has an elevator.
                [0-4152] paragraph
                  [0-4153] StaticText: If you are looking for a reasonably priced hostel and cannot find any in whole Amsterdam (especially on summer weekends), check the hostels in Purmerend (Hostel 45, City Trip) and Zaandam (Room Mate, City Trip). They lie outside of the Amsterdam city borders and so aren't displayed if looking for accommodation in "Amsterdam" at online travel agencies. Still from all places you reach the centre of Amsterdam in 30min by public transport.
              [0-4154] region: Stay safe
                [0-8749] div
                  [0-4155] heading: Stay safe
                  [0-4157] link: edit
                [0-4159] figure
                  [0-4160] link
                    [0-632] image
                  [0-8759] Figcaption
                    [0-4161] StaticText: The iconic flag of Amsterdam
                [0-4162] paragraph
                  [0-4163] StaticText: It might surprise some visitors, but Amsterdam is one of Europe's safest cities. It has an overall easy-going, laid-back feel and crime is not common. Amsterdam is female friendly, women can easily travel alone here and feel comfortable and safe. Gay and lesbian travellers also have little to worry about. However, you should take normal precautions against scams, pickpockets and baggage theft, especially in the main shopping streets, in trams and trains, at stations, and anywhere where tourists congregate.
                [0-4164] paragraph
                  [0-4165] StaticText: What looks like a footpath, especially along a canal bank, may be a
                  [0-4166] StaticText: bike lane
                  [0-4167] StaticText: . Bike lanes are normally marked by red/purple tiles or asphalt, and a bike icon on the ground. However, the colour fades over time, so you might miss the difference. Don't expect cyclists to be kind to pedestrians: some consider the sidewalk an extension of the road, to be used when it suits them. Never stay or walk on the bike path or street for extended periods of time, as you will be greeted only by angry bell ringing. Keep in mind that for many Amsterdammers, the bike is their main means of transportation.
                [0-4168] paragraph
                  [0-4169] StaticText: Watch out for
                  [0-4170] StaticText: trams
                  [0-4171] StaticText: when crossing the street. Taxis are also allowed to use some tram lanes, and even if not allowed, they often use them anyway. If you're driving, always give way to trams unless you're driving on a priority road.
                [0-4172] region: Canals
                  [0-8763] div
                    [0-4173] heading: Canals
                    [0-4175] link: edit
                  [0-4177] paragraph
                    [0-4178] StaticText: Amsterdam's canals are picturesque and full of fun - but are also (by far) the single biggest cause of death to tourists in Amsterdam. On average, about 25 people drown every year in the canals, almost all of them tourists. Invariably the victims are male and fall in while attempting to urinate in the canal - often the bodies are found with open fly. Typically, there is a lot of alcohol involved, sometimes mixed with other drugs. There is some speculation that fainting due to dropping blood pressure caused by the combination of relaxation from relieving oneself and sudden exposure to cold may be involved, but generally being blind drunk and completely unstable is a perfectly adequate explanation. So: peeing in a canal is not only unhygienic and antisocial, it's also potentially lethal if you're under the influence. Please pee in the place you are drinking or failing that at an outdoor urinal. If you really can't find one, do it against a tree (risking a fine) rather than in a canal (risking your life).
                [0-4179] region: Neighbourhoods
                  [0-8772] div
                    [0-4180] heading: Neighbourhoods
                    [0-4182] link: edit
                  [0-4184] paragraph
                    [0-4185] StaticText: The city centre is generally safe. However, there are differences between the neighbourhoods. For instance, Leidseplein and Rembrandtplein are the tourist traps of Amsterdam. They have relatively high prices with lots of scams. Zeedijk and Warmoesstraat had a reputation for gang violence and riots in the 1970s and 1980s. However, the security situation has improved significantly, and now they are safe to visit.
                  [0-4186] paragraph
                    [0-4187] StaticText: Be cautious in the
                    [0-4188] StaticText: Red-Light District
                    [0-4189] StaticText: . All kinds of people walk around there during the day, including families with children, but the area does attract seedier visitors and vagrants after sunset. As a tourist hotspot, the area attracts a lot of pickpockets.
                    [0-4190] StaticText: Do not take photographs of the prostitutes
                    [0-4191] StaticText: , you will be yelled at or worse. Groups of women visiting the Red-Light District at night might feel harassed in the aggressive environment, though this is said to be the safest area because of the police presence. Keep to main streets and groups. Although not really dangerous, women might want to avoid the narrow lane north of the Oude Kerk after dark, as the atmosphere can be quite intimidating.
                  [0-4192] paragraph
                    [0-4193] StaticText: Other areas in the city centre are mostly safe, but can get pretty much deserted after midnight, so you might want to avoid walking alone there at night. This is also true for the Kalverstraat and Nieuwendijk, even though shops are lit all night.
                  [0-4194] paragraph
                    [0-4195] StaticText: The outer boroughs have profound differences in safety levels.
                    [0-4196] link: Nieuw-West
                    [0-4198] StaticText: (especially Osdorp) and
                    [0-4199] link: Zuidoost
                    [0-4201] StaticText: still have a bruised image regarding violence and harassment. Urban renewal projects have improved conditions, but you should still be aware of the situation.
                    [0-4202] link: Noord
                    [0-4204] StaticText: also has some rougher neighbourhoods, but the rural parts are safe.
                    [0-4205] link: Oost
                    [0-4207] StaticText: is largely safe, but there are some neighbourhoods east of Oosterpark where some travelers might not feel comfortable.
                    [0-4208] link: Zuid
                    [0-4210] StaticText: is perfectly safe, even at night.
                  [0-4211] paragraph
                    [0-4212] StaticText: Neighbourhoods with a bad reputation might still be worth seeking out, but be cautious at day and avoid at night. As most tourists only visit the city centre and Zuid, they do not have much to worry about except for the usual precautions (e.g. scams and pickpockets).
                [0-4213] region: Cannabis and other drugs
                  [0-8783] div
                    [0-4214] heading: Cannabis and other drugs
                    [0-4216] link: edit
                  [0-4218] paragraph
                    [0-4219] StaticText: It cannot be denied that many tourists come to Amsterdam for the coffeeshops. If you're not a smoker, and you really want to try, start with something light, make sure you don't have an empty stomach, and don't combine it with any other drugs or intoxicants, including alcohol. Be forthright with the counter person about your inexperience, they see it all the time. Go with an experienced person if you can. Regardless of the strength, your first experience can be quite a sensation at first, but will quickly decrease in intensity. You may want to plan to return to your hotel and "hole up" for a couple of hours until you become comfortable with the feeling. If you do find yourself too strongly under the influence—feeling nauseated, woozy or faint—drink orange juice or eat something sweet like cookies or candy, and get fresh air. Dutch-grown
                    [0-4220] StaticText: nederwiet
                    [0-4221] StaticText: (a.k.a. super skunk) is much stronger than you might expect, even if you are experienced. The THC level can be as high as 25%.
                  [0-4222] paragraph
                    [0-4223] StaticText: Quality varies. Coffeeshops aimed at tourists are more likely to have overpriced and poor quality products. A simple rule of thumb is: if the place looks good and well-kept, chances are their wares will be good as well. Don't just enter a coffeeshop being overwhelmed that it's possible at all to buy and consume cannabis openly: be discerning as to the quality. Coffeeshops sell only soft drugs such as marijuana and hash—asking for other drugs is pointless because coffeeshops are watched closely by the authorities, and nothing will get them closed faster than having hard drugs for sale.
                  [0-4224] paragraph
                    [0-4225] StaticText: There's a small chance you will be approached by people offering to sell you hard drugs in the street, especially as you are walking through the Red-Light District. Ignoring (or failing that, a firm refusal) is enough—they will not pester you. The selling of drugs in the street is illegal and often dangerous; moreover, the drugs sold to strangers are usually fake. When they invite you to see the goods, they can lure you into a narrow street and rob you.
                  [0-4226] paragraph
                    [0-4227] StaticText: So-called
                    [0-4228] StaticText: smartshops
                    [0-4229] StaticText: do not sell any illegal products, but a range of dietary supplements, including 'herbal ecstasy'—a legal attempt at an ecstasy pill alternative which is a complete waste of money with various more or less obscure psychedelic herbs. The usage of
                    [0-4230] StaticText: magic mushrooms
                    [0-4231] StaticText: has been forbidden since 2008, but magic truffles (also containing psilocybin) remain legal. They can cause problems, as people often underestimate their strength. Psilocybin mushrooms have few physical risks attached to them, but can have a very strong psychological effect, which can either be great or very distressing. This is largely unpredictable, but is influenced by your own mindset (e.g. if you are relaxed, have any serious worries, history of mental illness, etc.) and your surroundings (e.g. if you feel comfortable and safe in them).
                  [0-4232] paragraph
                    [0-4233] StaticText: The first time you try this should always be in a familiar and trusted environment, not on the streets of an unfamiliar city. If you do decide to try, please get informed first by asking for information from the smartshop attendants. Most recommended is experimenting in your own room, or a quiet place away from traffic, with a sober and trusted friend around who can help you if you need. Make sure that being intoxicated will not endanger your safety, or that of anybody else.
                  [0-4234] paragraph
                    [0-4235] StaticText: If you're not sure of how much to take, take a small dose. Then you'll know what your "tolerance" level is. Never take more than one packet of mushrooms—usually half is good for your first time. A good smart shop can give you more information about this.
                  [0-4236] paragraph
                    [0-4237] StaticText: Since 2023, smoking cannabis on the street is banned in the Red Light District to reduce nuisance for residents.
                [0-4238] region: Pharmacies
                  [0-8795] div
                    [0-4239] heading: Pharmacies
                    [0-4241] link: edit
                  [0-4243] paragraph
                    [0-4244] StaticText: Community pharmacies can be found via
                    [0-4245] link: Apotheek.nl
                    [0-4247] StaticText: (in Dutch). Most pharmacies close between 17:00 and 18:00. The
                    [0-4248] link: Leidsestraat Apotheek
                    [0-4250] StaticText: in the Leidsestraat is open daily until 20:00.
                    [0-4251] link: Apotheek OLVG West
                    [0-4253] StaticText: is open 24 hours per day.
                  [0-4254] paragraph
                    [0-4255] StaticText: Some basic OTC drugs can be bought e.g. in
                    [0-4256] link: Kruidvat
                    [0-4258] StaticText: or
                    [0-4259] link: Etos
                    [0-4261] StaticText: (drugstore/chemist) and
                    [0-4262] link: Albert Heijn
                    [0-4264] StaticText: or
                    [0-4265] link: Jumbo
                    [0-4267] StaticText: (supermarkets).
              [0-4268] region: Connect
                [0-8805] div
                  [0-4269] heading: Connect
                  [0-4271] link: edit
                [0-4273] region: Internet
                  [0-8814] div
                    [0-4274] heading: Internet
                    [0-4276] link: edit
                  [0-4278] paragraph
                    [0-4279] StaticText: The first Internet cafes in the country opened in Amsterdam, but they vanished as quickly as they appeared. Only a few smaller Internet cafes remain in the
                    [0-4280] link: Binnenstad
                    [0-4282] StaticText: . Outside of it, you might want to try your luck at one of the phone shops (
                    [0-4283] StaticText: belwinkels
                    [0-4284] StaticText: ) that cater to immigrant communities, but they usually have only one or two terminals.
                  [0-4285] paragraph
                    [0-4286] StaticText: Free Wi-Fi is provided at
                    [0-4287] StaticText: OBA
                    [0-4288] StaticText: public libraries and municipal district offices. Library workstations are available for a fee (or for free with an OBA card).
                  [0-4289] paragraph
                    [0-4290] StaticText: If you bring a laptop, many hotels in the city offer Wi-Fi for guests, but check in advance as some places still charge high fees, while cheaper hotels and hostels may have no Internet service at all. Several fast food chain restaurants and an ever increasing number of cafés and restaurants offer free Wi-Fi for guests, although you are typically expected to order a drink. Shops like
                    [0-4291] StaticText: Albert Heijn
                    [0-4292] StaticText: supermarkets also provide Wi-Fi service. Speed and stability obviously differ per place.
                  [0-4293] paragraph
                    [0-4294] StaticText: All Dutch providers (KPN, Vodafone and Odido) have wide 5G coverage in Amsterdam. Be advised that you could incur steep data charges when roaming on a non-EU cellular plan.
                [0-4295] region: Telephone
                  [0-8826] div
                    [0-4296] heading: Telephone
                    [0-4298] link: edit
                  [0-4300] paragraph
                    [0-4301] StaticText: The country code for the Netherlands is
                    [0-4302] StaticText: 31
                    [0-4303] StaticText: and Amsterdam's area code is
                    [0-4304] StaticText: 020
                    [0-4305] StaticText: . You only need to dial the 0 if you're calling from within the Netherlands.
                  [0-4306] paragraph
                    [0-4307] StaticText: Public phone boxes
                    [0-4308] StaticText: have been taken out of service. If you need to make a call and do not have access to a phone, it is best to go to a
                    [0-4309] StaticText: phone shop
                    [0-4310] StaticText: (
                    [0-4311] StaticText: belwinkel
                    [0-4312] StaticText: ). Phone shops can be found all over the city. Outside the city centre, they mostly serve immigrants calling their home country at cheap rates.
                  [0-4313] paragraph
                    [0-4314] StaticText: The major mobile operators are KPN, Odido and VodafoneZiggo. If you have a simlock-free mobile phone suitable for European networks, consider buying a
                    [0-4315] StaticText: prepaid simcard
                    [0-4316] StaticText: . You can buy these in electronics stores, phone shops or brand stores of one of the three large providers.
              [0-4317] region: Cope
                [0-8841] div
                  [0-4318] heading: Cope
                  [0-4320] link: edit
                [0-4322] paragraph
                  [0-4323] StaticText: Many people choose to visit Amsterdam because of its reputation for tolerance and progressivism. Prostitution is legal and licensed in the Netherlands, so window prostitution is very visible in some areas of Amsterdam. The possession and consumption of small quantities of cannabis and hash, while it is illegal, is tolerated by authorities (the policy of
                  [0-4324] StaticText: gedogen
                  [0-4325] StaticText: ). Coffeeshops are allowed to sell cannabis and hash for personal use, and Amsterdam has hundreds of these scattered over the city.
                [0-4326] paragraph
                  [0-4327] StaticText: This does not mean that you can get away with anything in Amsterdam. In any case, public attitudes and official policy have hardened compared to some tourist perceptions. The number of coffeeshops has decreased significantly and new laws forbid the selling of dried hallucinogenic mushrooms. Window prostitution outside the Oudezijds Achterburgwal is slowly but surely being phased out by the local authorities.
                [0-4328] paragraph
                  [0-4329] StaticText: Depending on your viewpoint some people will consider Amsterdam an unwholesome city whereas other people will find the relaxed attitudes refreshing. If you avoid the Red Light District, Amsterdam is an excellent family destination.
                [0-4330] paragraph
                  [0-4331] StaticText: Since the 2000s tourism to Amsterdam has exploded and the city now suffers from
                  [0-4332] StaticText: overtourism
                  [0-4333] StaticText: . As a tourist you might be met with hostility. Avoiding a few faux pas helps diminishing this risk. Don't walk on cycling lanes or cycling tracks but stick to the pavement. Don't go around brawling, and don't drink in public. Avoid the Red Light District, and consider another destination for your bachelor(ette) party. If you're going for the monuments and can't cope with mass tourism, remember there are many smaller but similar cities in the Netherlands, like
                  [0-4334] link: Utrecht
                  [0-4336] StaticText: ,
                  [0-4337] link: Haarlem
                  [0-4339] StaticText: , and
                  [0-4340] link: Delft
                  [0-4342] StaticText: .
                [0-4343] paragraph
                  [0-4344] StaticText: Even though Amsterdam is the capital of the Netherlands, most embassies are in
                  [0-4345] link: The Hague
                  [0-4347] StaticText: , as is the government.

                [0-1134] paragraph
                  [0-1135] StaticText: Amsterdam
                  [0-1136] StaticText: is the capital of the
                  [0-1137] link: Netherlands
                  [0-1139] StaticText: . It is known for the canals that cross the city, its impressive architecture, museums and art galleries, its notorious red light district, and more than 1,500 bridges.
                [0-1140] paragraph
                  [0-1141] StaticText: The city has earned the title of
                  [0-1142] StaticText: Venice of the North
                  [0-1143] StaticText: for a good reason: few other cities have intricate web of canals, exquisite architecture, and a staggering collection of over 1500 bridges weave an undeniable charm. Whether you're here for the rich cultural heritage, the vibrant nightlife, or the serene alleyways, Amsterdam's magnetic pull is universal.
                [0-772] paragraph
                  [0-1144] StaticText: Although once an innocuous and humble fishing village during the late 12th century, Amsterdam catapulted into global prominence during the 17th century as a bustling trading hub. The city's evolution birthed iconic districts like Jordaan and the Canal Belt, the latter earning UNESCO World Heritage status in 2010. The 19th and 20th centuries ushered in expansion, punctuated by modernist districts.

                [0-1294] paragraph
                  [0-1295] StaticText: With a population surpassing 934,000 in 2025 – and soaring well past a million when you account for the immediate surroundings – Amsterdam unquestionably holds the crown as the Netherlands' largest city. Numbers aside, Amsterdam is the financial, cultural, and creative heart of the nation. English is widely spoken and understood by almost everyone, so language barriers are rarely an issue for travellers.
                [0-1296] region: Orientation
                  [0-6441] div
                    [0-1297] heading: Orientation

                      [0-1303] StaticText: Corner of Keizersgracht and Reguliersgracht
                  [0-1304] paragraph
                    [0-1305] StaticText: The "Amsterdam" that most visitors experience is the city centre, the semi-circle with Centraal Station at its apex. It corresponds to the city as it was around 1850. Five major concentric canals ring the Binnenstad: Singel, Herengracht, Keizersgracht, Prinsengracht and Singelgracht, together forming the Canal District. Other districts inside the city centre are the Jordaan, a former working class area now popular with yuppies, and Plantage, a leafy and spacious area with botanical gardens and the zoo. The Nassaukade, Stadhouderskade and Mauritskade surround the city centre and mark the location of the former city moat and fortifications. Almost everything outside this line was built after 1870.
                  [0-1306] paragraph
                    [0-1307] StaticText: The semi-circle is on the south side of the IJ, which is often called a river but more exactly is an estuary. Going east from Centraal Station, the railway passes the artificial islands of the redeveloped Eastern Docklands. North of the IJ is mainly housing, although a major dockland redevelopment has started there too.
                  [0-1308] paragraph
                    [0-1309] StaticText: The river Amstel flows into the city from the south. Originally, it flowed along the line Rokin-Damrak. The dam in the Amstel, which gives the city its name, was located under the present Bijenkorf department store near Dam Square. The original settlement was on the right bank of the Amstel, on the present Warmoesstraat: it is therefore the oldest street in the city. The city has expanded in all directions, except to the northeast of the A10 ring motorway. That area is a protected rural landscape of open fields and small villages considered a part of the Waterland region.
                  [0-1310] paragraph
                    [0-1311] StaticText: The radius of the semi-circle is about 2
                    [0-1312] StaticText: 
                    [0-1313] StaticText: km. All major tourist destinations, and most hotels, are located inside it or just outside it. As a result, a large swathe of Amsterdam is not visited by the average tourist: at least 90% of the population lives outside this area. Most economic activity in Amsterdam—the offices of the financial sector, the port—is near or outside the ring motorway, which is 4–5
                    [0-1314] StaticText: 
                    [0-1315] StaticText: km from the centre.
                  [0-1316] paragraph
                    [0-1317] StaticText: The expansion of Amsterdam outside the ring motorway and the expansion of activity outside the city centre is redefining what locals consider the 'central area' of Amsterdam. Zuid, especially with the construction of the Noord/Zuidlijn and the Zuidas, is becoming more and more important in the daily lives of the locals. Its significance for tourists has increased by the now completed reconstruction work on the Museumplein and the adjoining museums.

                  [0-1326] paragraph
                    [0-1327] StaticText: Amsterdam was first referred to as
                    [0-1328] StaticText: Aemstelledamme
                    [0-1329] StaticText: ("dam on the Amstel") in 1204, and known as
                    [0-1330] StaticText: Aemsterdam
                    [0-1331] StaticText: by 1327. It was first part of Utrecht, and around 1300 Gwijde van Henegouwen, bishop of Utrecht, gave Amsterdam city rights. After his death, the city was inherited by Count William III and became a part of Holland. Two fires swept the city in 1421 and 1452, and few wooden buildings from this period remain. A notable exception is the
                    [0-1332] StaticText: Houten Huis
                    [0-1333] StaticText: (Wooden House) at the Begijnhof.
                  [0-1334] paragraph
                    [0-1335] StaticText: In 1558, the Dutch started to revolt against the Spanish as the local nobility demanded more political power and religious freedom. Amsterdam supported the Spanish, but as it became more and more isolated and trade suffered accordingly, it switched sides in 1578. A relative freedom of religion emerged in the newly established Dutch Republic, and many migrants sought refuge in Amsterdam, including Jews from the Iberian Peninsula, merchants from Antwerp and
                    [0-1336] StaticText: Huguenots
                    [0-1337] StaticText: (French Protestants). Catholicism could not be practiced openly.
                  [0-1338] paragraph
                    [0-1339] StaticText: Amsterdam prospered in the 17th century and became one of the world's great cities. A global trading network and overseas possessions made Amsterdam the centre of shipping in Europe and the world's leading financial centre. The arts flourished too, with great painters like Rembrandt producing works that are widely acclaimed as of this day. The city expanded outside of its original boundaries as the Canal Belt was constructed for wealthy merchants and the Jordaan for the working class. Immigrants formed the majority of the population and there was a strong immigration from Lutheran Protestant Germans.
                  [0-1340] paragraph
                    [0-1341] StaticText: The Dutch Republic was not a unitary state, but a confederation in which the independent provinces and the larger cities were politically autonomous. There was a strong animosity between the Orange faction with its power base in The Hague and the republican faction with Amsterdam as its most outspoken representative, up to the point that the city was beleaguered by the army. The Orange faction supported the idea of hereditary political leadership vested in the princes of Orange as Stadtholders, while the republican faction supported civic independence. This long-standing culture of republicanism and non-conformism against the political elites in The Hague exists to this day.
                  [0-1342] figure

                  [0-1345] paragraph
                    [0-1346] StaticText: The 18th and 19th centuries were a turbulent period for Amsterdam. The economy suffered from decreased trade opportunities with the colonies and ongoing wars with the United Kingdom and France. Napoleon's brother Louis was crowned King of Holland in 1806 and took possession of the city hall on Dam Square, from then on referred to as the Royal Palace. The Netherlands was fully annexed by France in 1810, and Napoleon crowned Amsterdam "third city" of the French Empire. Prussian and Russian troops liberated the Netherlands, but it remained a unitary state and a monarchy, that now included Belgium.

                    [0-1348] StaticText: While The Hague had functioned as
